articles.title: Xbox Elite 3 prototype pad leaks with tiny built-in screen
articles.summary: A Redditor has legit-looking photos of a prototype Xbox controller that’s almost certainly the Xbox Elite Series 3.
articles.body: Did a prototype Microsoft gamepad fall off the back of a truck? We can’t say, but a Redditor has legit-looking photos of a prototype Xbox controller that’s almost certainly the Xbox Elite Series 3. Incredibly, they claim they bought the pad for $200 on OfferUp. In May, a Brazilian regulator’s leaked images revealed that Xbox Elite 3 would have new two new scroll wheels on the bottom edge, a second wireless mode to connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming servers, and a new “Pair Button” that can also switch between those servers and your console. Where might that pair button live? Today, we have a possible answer: it might sit right next to the Xbox Elite 3’s built-in screen, a previously unrevealed feature. The screen looks almost exactly like the leaked diagram from May showing the mode switch dialogue, with a pair button at the left: [Image: The Anatel image from May, overlaid atop the new prototype controller photos. And if I’m not mistaken, the screen on Redditor ssuberlex’s controller is displaying the little XCloud rocket ship next to an Xbox Series X. The screen can apparently display other things, too. In another photo, it shows a URL that takes me to a Microsoft cloud resource I don’t have permission to view. That lends these images some extra credibility. Unfortunately, the Redditor says the controller doesn’t work. “It does not pair with an Xbox nor with a cable. Just the red light blinking but doesn’t do any thing wired or wireless,” they wrote. [Image: In other photos, we can see the controller’s new scroll wheels, its four rear paddles, its battery compartment, its carrying case, and a different detachable D-pad design than we saw in the May leak. The Redditor says the triggers are clicky when you lock them to the hair-trigger position. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: But beyond the screen, the most intriguing image is from inside the controller’s battery compartment. It appears Microsoft has made efforts to make this controller home repairable by including a QR code that presumably leads to a repair website, and accessible Torx T6 screws. [Image: Still, none of these features are for certain. The controller is clearly a prototype, with “NOT FOR SALE” labels on both the pad and its removable 5.8 watt-hour battery, and many placeholder ID numbers for various regulatory bodies. [Image: Tom Warren, The Verge’s Microsoft expert, says his sources believe this controller is still coming later this year.

articles.title: X-Men '97 Season 2 Finale Review: Why "Survival of the Fittest" Fails to Tie the Season Together
articles.summary: X-Men '97 again becomes a victim of its relentless pacing in the Season 2 finale, as the final battle with Apocalypse fails to impress.
articles.body:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 9!

At this point, it's officially safe to say that X-Men '97 Season 2 doesn't live up to the standard set by the first. The highs are just as high, as we saw in the stellar first half. But the whole thing fails to come together in a cohesive package. These final two episodes have really lost the plot where Apocalypse (Ross Marquand) is concerned, resulting in a finale that hits some of the right notes yet ultimately still fails to bring the season home.

It's tough to make sense of the handling of the Apocalypse storyline post-Episode 4. The character was such a driving force of the first four episodes, but he faded into the background after that point. Not that every installment needed Apocalypse as its focal point, but the series has really started to suffer from the lack of attention paid to the character in recent weeks. So much about his motivations and actions is unclear. That entire backstory regarding his love affair with Candra was treated as an afterthought in Episode 8.

So it is that when Apocalypse finally resurfaces to confront Professor Xavier (Marquand) and the X-Men in the finale, that reunion falls a little flat. All the momentum Season 2 built up around Apocalypse in those first four episodes has faded.

When we finally see the reborn Apocalypse square off against the X-Men here, it's a very brief and anticlimactic battle between good and evil. No sooner does Apocalypse get to stretch his new Cajun-y legs than the power-boosted Rogue (Lenore Zann) shows up to save the day. This is the payoff to the entire season? Compared to the epic spectacle that was the "Beyond Good and Evil" storyline from the original series, this feels pretty bland and small potatoes in comparison. It's just bizarre that Apocalypse's grand, millennia-spanning master plan boiled down to stealing Gambit's (A. J. LoCascio) body and hassling the X-Men for a few minutes.

It's really in the build-up to that final showdown where "Survival of the Fittest" actually shines. There we get an actual epic throwdown between the reunited X-Men on one side and the combined forces of X-Force and X-Factor on the other. The action flows hot and heavy here, but the real joy is in how this conflict pays off on a season's worth of buildup for characters like Cable (Chris Potter) and Polaris (Carolina Ravassa). Their conflicted loyalties add a nice, extra touch of tragedy to the entire battle. At a time when human/mutant relations have really soured, it's a terrible thing to see the X-Men and their ilk fighting amongst themselves. Awesome in that Staurday morning cartoon way, but terrible.

I'll also say that, as much as I was underwhelmed by Rogue becoming the deus ex machina that quickly resolves the Apocalypse conflict, this episode does tug at the heartstrings when it comes to the Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough) twist. We're at first left to assume that Rogue and Remy will be torn apart once more, only to realize that Kurt sacrificed himself for the sake of his beloved sister. The writers of this series clearly love this character deeply, and his last and greatest sacrifice feels like a fitting end to his deeply emotional journey. Assuming it is the end, anyway. Based on how the Celestials operate, I would think that they're less interested in acquiring one little death than they are a replacement for Apocalypse in his role as cosmic gardener.

Ultimately, I find myself wishing that Season 2 retained the 10-episode structure of the first, which could have allowed this episode to focus on the X-Men vs. X-Force & X-Factor conflict and the finale to better flesh out the Apocalypse side of things. Former head writer Beau DeMayo has offered some insight into what the original plans for Episode 10 involved , though, to be frank, it sounds like that would have compounded the problem rather than addressed it. Perhaps it's best that the series simply wipe its hands of Apocalypse and try to start fresh in Season 3. The post-credits scene certainly gives us some idea of what's coming, but that's a topic for another article.

articles.title: The Voice of The Witcher's Geralt Says He'd Sue Every Single AI Platform With His Voice on It 'Into the Ground' if He Could
articles.summary: Doug Cockle, the voice behind The Witcher’s Geralt, has hit out at AI platforms that feature his voice, saying he’d sue them if he could.
articles.body:
Doug Cockle, the voice behind The Witcher’s Geralt, has hit out at AI platforms that feature his voice, saying he’d sue them if he could.

Speaking to Polygon , Cockle called AI replications of his voice “the bugbear of my life,” and expressed concern at the technology being used to make Geralt say awful things, which might then mislead some into thinking Cockle had actually provided the voice.

“If I had the power, the money, and the influence, I would sue every single AI platform out there with my voice on it. I would sue them into the ground,” he said.

“More than money or anything else is that they could make Geralt say horrible things. They could make Geralt a racist. They could make him a misogynist. They could make him have political views that are absolutely horrific.

“I’m being a little bit passionate about this, but it is the bugbear of my life at the moment. There are people behind these voices. They’re not just digital imprints.”

Cockle has been a vocal critic of generative AI, telling IGN in 2023 that he was worried about people using it for nefarious purposes .

"AI is inevitable and developers will use AI. We are not 100% sure exactly what that means," Cockle said at the time. "They're already doing it in various ways, filling in background, NPC voices, and things like that, which is unfortunate because those voices were all human beings at one point, and the voices are all modelled on human beings. So they have taken someone's voice, put it into their database, digitized it and are using it to say things that the individual never said. There's something unethical about that and so there's a lot of debate going on."

Cockle was contacted by an AI company a few years ago who wanted to upload his Geralt voice to its database. "And I said no, and I still say no. But that's not because I don't like AI," he said.

"It's because I think with voice actors, particularly with voice actors who do main character roles, it is a reality that people are ripping our voices off. That's happening. It's happened to me on multiple occasions. I can't even police it because I would spend all my time policing this stupid stuff."

Even if people are using the voice with good intentions, like genuine fans making Witcher mods , it directly impacts voice actors, Cockle added. "Every time somebody does that, they're effectively robbing me of income, and not just me, any other voice actor who they do it with. We're all watching our voices get used in ways that we would rather they weren't."

It's when those using AI do have illicit purposes that it gets really scary though. "This is the bit that we really don't like about AI, is that if they can do it for things that are just commercially questionable, then they can do it with things that are politically or ethically bad," Cockle said.

"Somebody could use AI to produce something racist using Geralt's voice, using my voice, or just something against anything that most normal people think is good. That's where the AI gets dangerous. Fake news, false news, false opinions. We're seeing it with politicians now. People are putting things out there. So AI is not the problem. It's the people using AI."

Cockle continued: "It's changed a lot as well, because when The Witcher 3 came out, I don't think that people playing games, not that they weren't interested, but they didn't really think about who was voicing these characters. It wasn't something that was of great interest. But I've watched over the years, it has become more and more interesting to players and to fans who the people are behind these voices, and that's a fantastic thing. But it also means that those voices are much more personalized. It's not just Geralt. That is my voice."

Video game voice actors previously called out AI-generated explicit Skyrim mods , and Assassin's Creed Syndicate voice actress Victoria Atkin called AI-generated mods the “invisible enemy we're fighting right now” after discovering her voice was used by cloning software. Paul Eiding, the voice actor behind Colonel Campbell in the Metal Gear Solid series, also condemned its use .

The issue was raised again today when it emerged that Saber Interactive, the company behind Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2, had used ChatGPT for taxi game Rideshare Stimulator — although it denied replacing an actual human writer with the tech.

The question is, can voice actors actually do anything about it? In July last year, video game actors voted to end a year-long strike over AI protections, with about 2,500 members of U.S. union SAG-Aftra involved in the action against 10 of the biggest companies in the industry, including Activision and Electronic Arts. In a statement released after the vote to end the strike, the union said a new contract secured "consent and disclosure requirements for AI digital replica use."

That, however, doesn't prevent anyone from using the established AI platforms to create fake videos featuring well-known video game characters saying and doing pretty much anything they want.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Coyote vs. Acme Is an Amazingly Meta Answer to Corporate Shenanigans, and an Anvil-Dropping, Rocket-Skate-Wearing, Batman and Joker Dynamic Wrapped in a Legal Drama
articles.summary: Coyote vs. Acme shows why Looney Tunes are just as funny now as they’ve ever been, with a film that’s an amazingly meta answer to corporate shenanigans, and an hilarious anvil-dropping, rocket-skate-wearing, Batman and Joker dynamic wrapped in a legal drama.
articles.body:
Coyote vs. Acme will be released in theaters on August 28.

Looney Tunes have been around since the ’30s. That’s almost 100 years, so it’s safe to say they’ve seen it all. That creators are still finding a way to make Bugs, Daffy and the rest continually fun and relevant is frankly pretty wild.

With Coyote vs. Acme, writer Samy Burch and director Dave Green have figured out a way to do it again. Tired of being exploded, bludgeoned and stranded in mid-air at high altitudes with nothing but the canyon floor distantly beneath him, Wile E. Coyote decides to sue Acme, the iconic company behind all the insane products he uses to not catch the Road Runner.

It’s a premise built on pain, suffering and pathological repetition that generations of humanity have found hilarious… myself included.

When he tracks down Will Forte’s Kevin Avery, a billboard-famous personal injury lawyer looking to do the bare minimum to get by in life relatively undetected,the movie turns into equal parts courtroom drama, corporate intrigue and dry absurdist comedy. It’s A Few Good Men by way of Who Framed Roger Rabbit and it works on just about every level.

Everything from the products themselves – from Acme brand canned lions to dehydrated boulders to the old reliable metal pellets mixed in with bird seed and a book titled How to Wait Around Dramatically, – to the characters named in honor of original Looney Tunes creatives Tex Avery, Chuck Jones and Michael Maltese, the details in the film are on point. The film is a mix of classic Looney Tunes gags with a more modern comedic sensibility, and it proves not only that Looney Tunes have always had that going for them, but also the filmmakers behind Coyote vs. Acme understand this and can add to it.

But Coyote and Road Runner are a very short form tradition. Stacking a narrative on top of a popular but story-less property is a phenomenon that The LEGO Movie perfected and plenty of would-be franchises have tried to imitate in the years since. Pianos being dropped on heads is all well and good for a few minutes at a time, but the real challenge with making a feature-length version is figuring out what can be interesting for an hour and a half. The answer for Coyote vs. Acme isn’t just the legal backdrop; it’s the weird psychological motivation behind Wile E. Coyote’s decades-long determination to catch Road Runner.

The film treats Coyote with no small amount of sadness. There’s a genuine obsession to what the Tune is doing with his life in the desert. Living in a cave, surrounded by blueprints of all his failed plans, Wile E. Coyote is the Joker to Road Runner’s Batman. Or vice versa, depending on who you’re rooting for. Ultimately, however, this is Will Forte’s movie as well, and as a two-hander with an animated coyote, the pair of them form a legitimately engaging emotional core. They both grow and learn and all that junk, but before you start thinking that a Looney Tunes movie is taking itself too seriously, I can assure you it does not. In the balancing act of adding enough heart to hang a whole story from while not shoving something so gauche as a “theme” down our throats, Coyote vs. Acme nails it.

Yes, it’s a story about becoming the best version of yourself, about trying over and over again in the face of failure, pain and rejection because you know it’s the right thing to do. There’s a mystery to solve in a fight against a heartless corporation. But also Porky Pig is “here for the pyuh-p-pyuh-pyuh-p-pantsless modeling gig.”

The comedic timing at play is also excellent. The movie is not afraid of an awkward pause or rapid-fire sight gags. Every joke is treated with exactly what it needs. This is due in large part to the supporting cast. John Cena as Acme’s shameless in-house counsel Buddy Crane does exactly what he needs to. Ditto Lana Condor as Avery’s idealistic, recent law school grad. They’re both very good and carry their scenes with humor and weight as needed, but the funniest non-animated cast members have way fewer lines than either of them.

Luis Guzman as the trial judge who doesn’t want any silliness in his courtroom, Martha Kelly as an employee of Avery’s law firm who might not make it back from her mini-golf tournament this weekend, and P.J. Byrne as an Acme stooge and Cena sycophant all bring a ton to this movie in small doses. For me, those are the types of characters to keep an eye on. They’re the ones that speak to how effective a movie like this is. When there are entire moments built around the supporting cast members that survive the editing process, it means the filmmakers knew what they were doing during casting, production and post.

We also have to talk about the meta narrative at play with this movie. Coyote vs. Acme famously slipped the noose when Warner Bros. boss David Zaslav tried to kill the movie to take a tax break. Thanks to the cast and crew and, frankly, most of us shouting about how dumb and tragic that would be, WB rethought the decision and Ketchup Entertainment stepped in to release the movie.

The film wasn’t written about that in the first place, but it is hilariously appropriate that a Looney Tunes movie about corporate shenanigans would fall victim to corporate shenanigans itself. There were a few touches most likely added in the aftermath of the Warner Bros. near-miss, like the “Based on a True Story” title card at the beginning of the film, and the jokes about WB being a wholly owned subsidiary of the Acme Corporation.

It’s a testament to the filmmakers trying over and over again, in the face of failure and rejection and corporate overreach, like the film’s central characters. Coyote vs. Acme is ironically the perfect movie to have survived that ordeal. It’s so perfect, the cynical side of me wonders if WB didn’t stage the whole thing as a publicity stunt. Who knows? Either way, it’s a layer of intrigue to this movie that fell on their heads like an anvil from the sky and the film does not waste the opportunity.

articles.title: The Latest One Piece Board Game Gives You 6 Bosses to Fight, But Kind of Feels Like It Plays Itself
articles.summary: The push-your-luck dice rolling can be fun with the right group, but One Piece: Escape from Egghead stumbles due to ambiguous rules, questionable designs, and mechanics that break at different player counts.
articles.body:
At this point, my adventure with the Straw Hat Pirates and One Piece has largely come vicariously through Kess’s board games, adapting parts of the various arcs. The latest of those is Kess's take on the Egghead arc with One Piece: Escape from Egghead, a push-your-luck dice roller that sees up to four players racing to escape the island. Unfortunately, out of the publisher’s pirate-y offerings, Escape from Egghead falls at the bottom of the list and left me underwhelmed, reminding me of the inescapable truth of anime – not all arcs are created equal.

One Piece: Escape from Egghead Board Game

Escape from Egghead reminds me a lot of the games I played growing up, where there wasn’t much player interaction and the games would sort of play themselves. Leaning heavily into randomness, nearly every aspect of Egghead, from where you can go, if you succeed, and even what help you may get, is largely out of your hands. It all comes down to a roll of the dice or what card gets drawn. This won’t be the game for folks who enjoy much strategy in their board games .

The board is split up into six paths, composed of three spaces, each leading to a boss. During setup, you shuffle and place facedown the bosses and the route’s tiles, before flipping over the first tile. Then on your turn, you roll two or three dice whose values will determine which routes Luffy and Bonney can take, with the remaining die adding to your food total – a resource that you can spend to boost your rolls during the following “Rush” phase.

This second phase is where a majority of the “action” takes place, which really just amounts to rolling dice and seeing if you surpass a number. Each of the route tiles features an enemy for your character and an associated challenge rating for you to get past. Passing just involves rolling a die and spending food to beat the route's challenge number; doing so gives you some sort of reward like additional food or a reroll token. From there, you either repeat the process or set your flag down, which lets you start your future rushes down that route further along, in future turns.

The bosses at the end of each path play out the same, except there is usually some sort of restriction or challenge. St. Saturn for instance has an increased challenge rating of 11 if you enter his space with an odd amount, whereas if you face him with an even amount, it’s only 9. Why is that the case? I have no idea. A quick read through from the character’s page on the One Piece Wiki did not share insight as to why this man has an aversion to odd numbers, and it makes me curious how much thought was put into best representing the characters and their quirks.

Once you have escaped a route’s boss, you place a marker on one of the rewards and return to base. Each boss only has so many open spots to be claimed, meaning if there is no reward to be claimed, the rules state “you can no longer escape from the route”. The rulebook doesn’t clarify whether the route becomes permanently closed or if the boss can still be defeated but you simply wouldn’t get a reward.

This sort of ambiguity underlines my biggest issue with Egghead: the whole thing just feels a bit runny and undercooked. From typos in the instruction manual, missing rule clarifications and examples, even down to the board’s design, it’s hard not to feel like this was pushed out the door too soon without getting a final pass through.

As for the board itself, its outward expanding routes are visually interesting and catch the eye, but this leads to two unnecessary problems. First, it results in a larger table footprint than the board really needs. Worse, it causes an unfortunate situation where the closest tiles to the players are all upside down. Unless you intend to play this on a large rotating lazy-susan or your players all love to read upside down, Egghead will require you to move around the table just to read the tiles you’re landing on.

I frequently found myself asking why couldn’t this game simply have six horizontal lines with the tiles connecting on their sides instead of tops and bottoms? This would serve the same function, and allow everything to be facing the players, making it take up far less space, and allow everything to be readable from a single direction.

Another rather odd aspect to Egghead is that, at least using the rules as written, playing at two players inadvertently removes the countdown timer from the equation. There are six Vegapunks that must all be flipped before the countdown timer starts, which can result in everyone losing. The game ends when the first player escapes three bosses. Put those two systems together and have yourself a situation where it is impossible to trigger that losing scenario. This doesn’t feel intentional either, and comes off more as “we didn’t test the game enough” since the stated objective in the instructions reads “Be the first player to escape from three different Bosses and leave Egghead Island before the Vegapunk Timer runs out.” Playing with two players basically erases everything after “and”.

The stated goal the game gives players is not only to escape three boss but ALSO to do so before the timer runs out. If the timer never starts, then half of the challenge is meaningless. As a homebrew rule, I would recommend adjusting the Vegapunk count per player counter (2 players / 4 punks, 3 players / 5 punks, 4 players / 6) just to keep that little bit of tension in the game.

One Piece: Escape from Egghead feels tailored toward the more casual general consumer crowd rather than the board game hobbyist. This is a “push your luck” dice rolling game that leans heavy into randomness and away from giving you much in the way of meaningful choices. Your only real choices come down to whether you want to roll more dice or not and which reward spot you take on the bosses. Everything else is out of your control.

I have enjoyed Kess’s other One Piece offerings like Luffy’s Bento Panic , and I'm excited for the full release of their big Dawn of Liberation game. Even here, I see the value in a good ol’ dice chucker game that you can just turn off your brain and enjoy. If that is what you’re looking for and you consider yourself a big One Piece fan, you may find some fun here with Egghead. That being said, it’s also hard to overlook the stumbles and some of the odd design choices the game makes, knocking it down a peg. While some homebrew fixes and adjustments can help patch the holes, Escape from Egghead is still a leaky ship.

Scott White is a freelance contributor to IGN, assisting with tabletop games and guide coverage. Follow him on X/Twitter or Bluesky .

articles.title: Reacher Season 4 Keeps the Action Coming But Makes Some Major Changes in the Source Material, Lee Child's Gone Tomorrow
articles.summary: Reacher Season 4 review: He’s good at not letting people get away with things.
articles.body:
Season 4 of Reacher premiered Wednesday, August 12, on Prime Video with the first three episodes; subsequent episodes debut each Wednesday until September 16.

Adapting Lee Child’s 13th Jack Reacher novel, Gone Tomorrow, was never going to be an entirely straightforward exercise in 2026. Obviously, I can’t quite explain why; if I did, non-readers would still be able to connect enough dots to ruin at least one of the twists in the latest live-action adventure of Prime’s premier skull-pounding ex-MP. Broadly, however, the backgrounds and motivations of Gone Tomorrow’s villains simply weren’t going to work in the present day, with 17 years having passed since the book’s publication.

As such, Reacher Season 4 takes more creative liberties than ever before while unfurling its eight-episode story. However, it doesn’t just change the entire aforementioned backstory and motivations of the core bad guys; it also weaves in a far grander ultimate threat as well as entire stretches of plot that are completely unique to the TV adaptation. The upshot is that this is perhaps the least predictable season yet for entrenched fans who’ve already devoured the novels. However, it’s also arguably the most frustrating, seeing as these alterations have resulted in the show sidelining at least a couple crucial components of the Reacher formula.

Season 4 finds Alan Ritchson’s always-wandering Jack Reacher in Philadelphia. The novel was set in New York, but Philadelphia seems similar enough; besides, Season 2 already did New York (despite the source novel for that being set in California). The long-running book series has seen Reacher in the Big Apple on multiple occasions, but it certainly wouldn’t make sense for the city to suddenly be the primary setting for half the Prime Video series aired to date.

At any rate, I will say that the “small town, big city, small town, and back again” cadence definitely doesn’t feel coincidental at this point, especially since we know that Season 5’s source novel — 2015’s Make Me — has already been locked in and will again return Reacher to small-town America. I continue to believe that it’s the right play to swing between backdrops; it makes the series feel like it’s truly shifting gears between seasons.

As Season 4’s story begins, Reacher finds himself drawn into a random encounter in a sparsely filled subway carriage, as his training compels him to approach a visibly distressed woman named Anna Merrick. She’s showcasing a number of signs that Reacher immediately finds impossible to ignore, but while his instincts initially steer him towards an incorrect assumption, Anna’s next move drags Reacher into a police investigation. This quickly widens into a twisted and wide-reaching conspiracy, with a shady government agency, hired mercenaries, a pair of foreign nationals, and a former special forces operator-turned-US congressman clashing with Reacher as they work to track down a USB drive Anna is purported to have had in her possession. This MacGuffin drives the bedlam (and the body count) for some time, until the season quickly mashes the throttle for an escalation that leaves the original novel in the rearview mirror. I can concede it makes for a more traditionally explosive television finale, but I’d argue that it arrives as a pretty worn out crescendo we’ve seen a hundred times before.

As with previous seasons, Reacher picks up a number of new allies, including Philly detective Tamara Green (GLOW’s Sydelle Noel) and Anna’s brother Jacob (Christopher Rodriguez-Marquette), who is a small-town cop himself. They’re actually a lot more present in this season than I’d expected considering Gone Tomorrow the novel is a slightly more solitary affair that sees Reacher slogging his way through most of the story’s encounters solo.

It’s a competent supporting cast, and their characters carry credibility as investigators thanks to their law enforcement background, but the only memorable standout is Tamara’s partner Docherty, played by veteran character actor Kevin Corrigan (True Romance, Superbad, The Pineapple Express). Corrigan absolutely nails his role as an exhausted veteran detective with limited patience for Reacher’s schtick. He doesn’t get a ton of screen time, but what he does receive is actually a little more in line with what I’d expected for the side characters this season.

Unfortunately, Season 4’s villains are far less convincing. They’re ruthless and awful — the perfect combination for a Jack Reacher death sentence — but they’re thinly drawn. It takes a while to wheel them out, but this is admittedly in line with the Gone Tomorrow novel. They don’t have much in the way of great dialogue; in fact, some of it is quite poor, with one particularly exposition-heavy exchange coming across as unnecessarily detailed and rather forced considering how long they’ve apparently known each other.

They also seem to have survived way longer than their decision-making skills should have allowed. At one stage, they bring literal knives to a gunfight, and only live because the script lets them monologue when the novel Reacher would have just made sure they were each shot in the face. Ritchson’s TV Reacher definitely also began life as an uncompromising force that doesn’t fight fair and never waits until the count of three, so scenes like this continue to play as disappointingly off-brand. I’m sorry, but knives do not move faster than bullets.

Fortunately, Season 4 still regularly lets its man mountain off the leash, and the best thing about the series unambiguously remains Ritchson’s Reacher himself and the crunching fight scenes he finds himself in. Reacher is still a principled yet completely remorseless killer when the situation requires, and I live for his largely emotionless pre- and post-action ultimatums. These quips are always delivered unironically with a mix of ice-cold military sternness and almost child-like honesty: “I’m good at not letting people get away with things,” he says early on. While his expressions are typically blank, they always leave me grinning, and I commend the show’s habit of wheeling them out at the perfect moments and not overusing them to the point of parody. Frankly, I love how uncomplicated they tend to be too; hell, Reacher’s remarks are at their very best when he loads the promise of a dramatically shortened lifetime of pain into a single word.

“What’s the signal?” asks one of Reacher’s allies as Reacher prepares to split from the group and attack an encroaching group of goons from behind. His reply is one, deeply satisfying word: “Screaming.”

articles.title: The next big indie game publisher is taking some exciting swings
articles.summary: Kinetic Publishing just hosted its first games showcase. Arguably the biggest announcement is that it’s publishing Sam Barlow’s next game, Precognition.
articles.body: Kinetic Publishing, a new indie publisher from the development team behind the co-op horror game Phasmophobia, just hosted its first games showcase, and it includes five ambitious new titles set to release in 2027 and 2028.  Perhaps the most significant announcement from Kinetic’s show is that it’s publishing the next game from Telling Lies and Immortality creator Sam Barlow, titled Precognition. (Barlow previously revealed the game as “Project C.”) Like other Barlow titles, Precognition will feature FMV-sequences and nonlinear storytelling. Here’s the setup: > Players take on the role of Diana, a woman who discovers she can receive visions of the future after an experimental implant is embedded into her brain. > Players will be tasked with exploring these visions of the future, focusing on specific moments and committing them to Diana’s memory in the present day. Prescience comes with consequences, however, and as soon as Diana commits a detail to memory, the very future ahead of her changes. Barlow and his studio, Half Mermaid Productions, are collaborating with film director Brandon Cronenberg (Infinity Pool, Possessor) on the game. It’s set to launch in spring 2028 on the Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X / S. [Image: The rest of the lineup shown off on Wednesday includes a mix of games across a few different genres. They’re all set to launch on Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X / S.  * Contact Protocol, from Cold Zephyr Games, is a “starship job simulator” where you play as a security officer that has to vet approaching starships. It’s scheduled to launch in spring 2027. * Crescent County, from Electric Saint, is a “cosy-with-bite slice-of-life game” where you build relationships on a magical island and use your Star Wars speeder-like “motorbroom” to make deliveries and race other characters. It’s planned for a summer 2027 release. * Shellbound, from Fake Lobster, is a Metroidvania that takes place on a giant, living snail. It’s set to launch in summer 2028. * Aether Wizard Life, from Vonder Games, is another cozy game, this one focused on being a wizard. Keep an eye out for it in autumn 2028. Kinetic announced its publishing arm back in January. It’s part of something of a trend of successful indie developers, like Palworld’s Pocketpair and Slay the Princess’ Black Tabby Games, that are using their financial success to help other game makers launch their own titles.

articles.title: Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth Feels Less Like a Board Game and More Like a Tabletop RPG Without a GM
articles.summary: Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth feels less like a board game and more like a fancy way to run a role-playing game without a GM.
articles.body:
If there’s one board game theme that rivals pleasing Renaissance-era nobles in popularity, it’s the works of H. P. Lovecraft. There’s just something about those tentacled horrors from outer space that seems to keep on appealing to tabletop adaptations. Just look at the ongoing acclaim heaped on Arkham Horror: The Card Game .

Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth is the latest game to join this crowded lineage. But it’s attempting to stand out by taking a different route to the majority of its sticky, ichorous peers. A leaflet in the box suggests that you might want to go buy not another Lovecraftian board game but the role-playing game based on his works: Call of Cthulhu . This is more of a storytelling game than a strategy game.

The box is so hefty that you might worry it could actually contain an avatar of Nyarthatolep, but you can lift the lid in safety: the weight comes from the inclusion of three big spiral-bound books that contain the text paragraphs you’ll be referring to during the game. They’re good quality and will absolutely stand to be bent and flipped through time and time again. What’s less inspiring is the sheets of errata stickers you’ll need to paste onto various entries to ensure you have all the options the designers intended.

The remainder of the weight is mostly from several decks of cards. There are square location cards that are used to build the map, tarot-sized encounter cards for the bad guys you can meet on your adventures, and several standard playing-card sized decks. These include condition cards to track the bad – and occasionally beneficial – things that can happen to your character and a ton of skill cards that you’ll play to meet challenges. Most of these cards are purely informational, with solid graphic design that favors function over form but the location cards are graced with darkly evocative artwork.

It’s a similar story for the selection of character boards and their accompanying punch-out standees, representing an excellent variety of character types in every sense of the word, brought to life nicely in all their 1920s glory. There are lots of other, more workmanlike tokens to punch out, too, for tracking various actions and statuses during play.

Alongside the weighty components is an innocuous-looking, lightweight rulebook that you’ll quickly find is poorly laid out and worded. Everything you need to play is in there, but you’ll need repeated puzzled flip-throughs during setup and the first few turns before everyone is comfortable with what’s going on.

Broadly, your group will choose one of three missions, which are best played in order, and which you’ll work together to complete. You place a starting location and objective card and read an introductory paragraph of text which explains the various options that you have in that location. Most of them require you to discard one of your character’s skill cards to do something, while others require you to pass a skill check. This involves characters, often more than one if working together, to discard cards either of the skill type required for one automatic “success” towards the target number, or a card of a similar type to get a dice to roll which may, or may not, generate a success. You need enough successes to pass the target number in order to succeed.

In addition to the dice you get by generating cards you will also always roll a red dice in these checks. This can give you an extra success, but it can also roll scary-looking symbols like skulls or tentacles. These cause the matching track to increment and, often, to cause you to flip to a paragraph in the book, triggering an event in the in-game narrative, usually an undesirable one.

Running out of cards also causes a time track to increment with similar paragraphs along the route, putting you under a bit of pressure to hurry along and achieve your objectives. It’s a neat way of giving your adventures a sense of time and dynamism as you move through the locations.

You’ll spend a lot of your time in Miskatonic Tales reading paragraphs, not only from the tracks but when you enter a new location and in describing the results of your actions, pass or fail. You can appoint one person to read these out to the group, or take turns, or there’s a free app to download which will do it for you with very questionable voice acting. The writing is fine: it’s not overloaded with the obscure adjectives that Lovecraft was fond of, nor is it lifeless, but it’s not especially inspiring, either. It’s just about enough to set the scene and keep you engaged.

Where the paragraphs really shine is in giving you options. The choose your own adventure books this style of play derives from often leave players feeling as though they’d like to do things that aren’t offered as choices. That rarely happens here: there are paragraphs to interact in different ways with pretty much everything described. Indeed there are too many options to explore them all without running down your time track dangerously fast. You’ll need to pick and choose what you do based on your curiosity and your objectives.

The trouble is that you don’t have very much else beyond those two things to guide your picks. Again, like the gamebooks it evokes, most of the decision-making happens in the dark as you have very little information on which to guess which options are better than others. You can’t even really strategize around the skill check system beyond a bit of risk-reward analysis. The closest the game comes to giving you meaningful decisions are your use of when to spend magic points which give you re-rolls, and when to use each character’s special abilities. As a result, this feels less like a board game and more like a particularly fancy way to run a role-playing game without a GM.

You don’t even get much strategy or tactics when it comes to combat. Encounters can either be fought with weapons, if you have them, or via a different skill, either of which is resolved with the standard dice-rolling skill check mechanism. That’s pretty much the only choice you get. Damage is taken off your character’s health or sanity values and you can also take hits to these tracks from accumulating status cards like panic or injury that are given out by in-game events. If either track runs down to zero, that investigator is out of the game.

Win or lose, one thing the plethora of exploration options gives you is a decent amount of replay value. There’s a ton of stuff to do in Miksatonic Tales and a second attempt at a scenario can work out very differently from the first. The game has a neat keyword system that tracks how past decisions can impact future situations although, as per most of the game, you have no way of knowing how this will play out. Many of the choices lead to blind alleys or horrible punishments you cannot anticipate, which can feel frustrating but it suits the source material well enough. What it lacks in strategy, it makes up for in anticipation. However, whether you’ll want to replay a scenario is a moot point as game times run long, much of which is taken up by players reading out text. You can “save” your game to stretch it across multiple sessions if needs be.

articles.title: Curry, Wembanyama o Edwards, entre los 'reyes' del NBA 2K27: Estos son los líderes en cada estadística del juego
articles.standfirst: 2K publicaba el top 10 de jugadores en diferentes aparatados
articles.summary: 2K publicaba el top 10 de jugadores en diferentes aparatados
articles.body: La NBA acabó la temporada anterior, la 25/26 por todo lo alto con el anillo de los New York Knicks. Pero esta temporada que viene, la 26/27, no ha empezado de diferente manera, ya que hemos tenido un inicio espectacular, primero con el draft en el que tres nuevos españoles han llegado a la mejor liga de baloncesto del planeta, Aday Mara, Sergio de Larrea y Baba Miller, y más tarde con una agencia libre que nos ha dejado movimientos históricos que prometen cambiar la competición por completo. Giannis Antetokounmpo aterrizando en los Miami Heat era el primer gran movimiento que veíamos en la NBA de cara a la temporada que viene, el que pensábamos que, de lejos, sería el más impactante, pero no. Ya que el bombazo de Jalen Brown y LeBron James fichando por Philadelphia 76ers han dado un vuelco radical a una conferencia este más fuerte de lo que estábamos acostumbrados a ver. Este inicio de temporada marcado por el draft y la agencia libre marca, como decíamos, el inicio de una nueva temporada en la NBA, pero el lanzamiento del NBA 2K también, ya que el mejor juego de la mejor liga de baloncesto del planeta sigue el ciclo de la competición. Y es que ya tenemos las primeras noticias sobre el NBA 2K27, como la portada de Victor Wembanyama, las primeras imágenes oficiales del videojuego, o, por supuesto, las primeras estadísticas de los jugadores. Como por ejemplo las medias de algunos jugadores, en concreto las de los rookies, los que llegan a la NBA este año con especial expectación y en la que no vemos a Aday Mara entre los 10 mejores de este año, algo que nos podíamos esperar ya que fue elegido en la posición números 12. Independientemente de esto, estos son los 10 mejores novatos de la NBA según las valoraciones de 2K27. Pero además de las medias también, como es tradición cada año, 2K publica el top 10 de jugadores en estadísticas concretas, sin importar la valoración general, solo ese apartado en concreto del jugador. Por eso, en los apartados defensivos siempre tenemos a algunos habituales que aparecen año tras año, auténticos especialistas en la defensa que copan estas listas. El primero de ellos, como no podía ser de otra manera si hablamos de tapones es Victor Wembanyama, el que con un 99 en este apartado cuenta con los mejores números en tapones, algo lógico pues es insuperable. Pero en la 'otra defensa', la del perímetro y los robos, también tenemos un claro vencedor, Ausar Thompson, el alero de los Pistons que es un muro, tanto en la realidad como en el videojuego. Pero en estas listas de defensores también tenemos a otros 'sospechosos habituales' como Kawhi Leonard, Derrick White, Dyson Daniels, Alex Caruso o Rudy Gobert, jugadores que siempre han estado entre los mejores defensores de la competición, también en el NBA 2K. Como no podía ser de otra manera, si hay mejores defensores también hay mejores atacantes, por lo menos si tenemos en cuenta solamente el tiro, y estos, por lo que vemos cada día en las pistas de la NBA son indiscutibles. Decimos esto porque como el mejor tirador de media distancia tenemos a Shai Gilgeous-Alexander con 99, algo lógico, ya que en la realidad parece que el canadiense no puede fallar desde esa zona. Y si esta estadística tenía un dominador claro la del triple más todavía, ya que si hay un especialista desde la línea de 3 puntos en la NBA, en toda la historia de la liga, ese es Stephen Curry, el base de los Warriors que con 99 de valoración en este apartado deja muy lejos al segundo de esta lista, Kon Knueppel, el que cuenta con un 94. Hablando de ataque, al igual que tenemos a los mejores tiradores, también tenemos a los mejores manejadores, esos jugadores que hacen lo que quieren cuando tienen el balón en las manos. Y al igual que Curry lleva siendo años el 'rey del triple', Kyrie Irving es el del manejo de balón, también este año en NBA 2K27 con una valoración en este apartado de 99. Pero si mezclamos esta gran habilidad y la potencia, la velocidad, es decir, el apartado de velocidad con el balón en las manos, también tenemos a un habitual en esta estadística, uno de esos jugadores que en cuanto tienen el balón en las manos son inalcanzables si 'arrancan la moto'. Hablamos de De'Aaron Fox, el que tiene un 97 en este apartado en NBA 2K27. Y para terminar vamos con el apartado más espectacular, tanto en la realidad como en el videojuego y este es el de los mates y el salto vertical, esta habilidad que hace que nos levantemos del asiento si de verdad un jugador lo domina. Como por ejemplo Amen Thompson, el alero de los Rockets que lidera la lista de salto vertical en el NBA 2K27 con un 99 en este apartado junto a Tobi Lawal, el de Dallas, que cuenta con los mismos números. Pero más espectacular es cuando el salto vertical acaba en canasta, en un mate espectacular, un apartado de juego que llama siempre mucho la atención y que es una de las cualidades de Anthony Edwards, el que lidera la lista de 'dunkers' de NBA 2K27 con un 97.

articles.title: Ni Hugo González ni Aday Mara, los españoles de la NBA se quedan fuera de 'las élites' del 2K27
articles.standfirst: Nuestros representantes en la mejor liga del mundo no están entre los mejores en el videojuego
articles.summary: Nuestros representantes en la mejor liga del mundo no están entre los mejores en el videojuego
articles.body: Como ocurre en cada inicio de la temporada de la NBA, el 2K, el mejor videojuego sobre la liga, también arranca una 'nueva vida' con el lanzamiento de una nueva edición. Y con este comienzo también tenemos mucha nueva información como por ejemplo los mejores jugadores del videojuego en cuanto a la valoración o los mejores jugadores en diferentes aspectos del juego como el tiro de tres, la defensa de perímetro o el manejo de balón, por ejemplo. Pues bien, de cara al NBA 2K27 tenemos malas noticias para nuestro país, por lo menos si hablamos de este videojuego, ya que ninguno de los españoles aparecen entre los mejores jugadores por valoración general, tanto en la lista global como la de los rookies, pero tampoco en los apartados de robos, tapones, defensa del perímetro, tiro de media distancia, tiro de tres, manejo de balón, velocidad con balón, salto vertical o mates, todas las categorías sobre las que tenemos rankings para 2K27. Y es que esta noticia pese a que sea negativa no nos pilla por sorpresa ya que ninguno tiene todavía esa consideración de estrella dentro de la liga. Pesa a esto podíamos pensar que por ejemplo Santi Aldama, un jugador bien considerado dentro de la NBA, podía estar entre los 100 mejores jugadores por media de la liga, y más viendo que los primeros en entrar en este top contaban solamente con un 81 de media. Pero además de este, si nos vamos a listas más específicas podíamos haber tenido representación como por ejemplo en la de los rookies, ya que Aday Mara, uno de los jugadores con más hype de este draft, elegido en el número 12, no se ha conseguido colar en el top 10 de novatos en 2K27. Y es que aunque quizá es soñar demasiado, el recién elegido por los Thunder podría haber tenido un hueco en el top 10 de taponadores por esa envergadura y capacidad para taponar tiros, aunque seguro que, aunque no esté ahora, lo veremos en un futuro. Para terminar nos vamos con Hugo González, el que ya en su primer año impresionó a toda la NBA por su capacidad de trabajo y defensa, por eso podíamos soñar con su presencia entre los 10 mejores de la liga en cuanto a robos, o mejor todavía, en defensa en el perímetro, la gran cualidad que ha mostrado el de los Celtics en su breve paso por la NBA, aunque, al igual que decíamos con Aday, si no está todavía en esta lista, estamos seguros de que lo veremos en el futuro.

articles.title: Strange New Worlds' Film Noir Episode Looks Cool, Sure, But Also Reminds Us That a Gimmick Is Not Enough to Carry an Hour of TV
articles.summary: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Episode 4 Recap and Review: “A Case of Chiaroscuro” is a high-concept, low-impact installment of Strange New Worlds that looks cool, sure, but also reminds us that a gimmick is not enough to carry an episode.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 4, “A Case of Chiaroscuro.”

Alright, here’s the thing about Strange New Worlds. For whatever reason, at some point showrunners Akiva Goldsman and Henry Alonso Myers decided that gimmick episodes were what this show needed. After a brilliant first season of adventure-of-the-week episodes, Season 2 featured occasional segments like “Those Old Scientists,” a crossover with the animated series Lower Decks , and “Subspace Rhapsody,” a musical episode, which lit a fire under the notion of what a modern episode of Star Trek could be. And that was great.

But somewhere along the way, the gimmicks became the focus, and frankly, they’ve grown kind of tiresome. I was really hoping with Season 4 that we’d just get back to regular weekly adventures. So when this week’s episode, “A Case of Chiaroscuro,” began and everything was in black and white, my mind immediately went to Yellow Alert. By the time we were on Mat'aar XII, the planet of the week (which is a kind of throwback to a film noir and/or Casablanca world), my inner Red Alert was in full effect. IT’S ANOTHER GIMMICK EPISODE.

When a newly promoted Commander Una Chin-Riley (Rebecca Romijn) leads an away team of Dr. M'Benga (Babs Olusanmokun) and Ensign Uhura (Celia Rose Gooding) to retrieve a probe that’s strayed into Klingon space, the group find themselves stuck on Mat'aar XII, where not only does everything appear to be black and white to our heroes (due to the infrared something something radiation of the system), but also you have to dress up like knock-off Humphrey Bogarts and Carmen Sandiegos in order to fit in.

Look, it’s a cute enough idea I suppose. The Original Series did go to a gangster planet after all. And the visuals of the episode are pretty cool. But as “A Case of Chiaroscuro” labors through its beats to hit the tropes of the genre(s) it’s working to imitate, the hour just winds up feeling like a Cinema Studies 101 midterm paper: High-contrast and shadowy black and white photography? Check. Doppelgänger characters? Check. A central bar/cafe where conspirators and their foes can congregate? Check. Corrupt local authorities? Check. And so on and so on. The thing is, like that middling paper from the kid who only half paid attention in class, the episode really gets its film noir chocolate mixed up in its wartime/romance film peanut butter.

But whatever, let’s not quibble about that. The real problem here is that Una’s struggle isn’t really fleshed out enough. I understand that she’s torn between wanting to help the local resistance fighters who are pushing against the Klingon occupation they are enduring, and I also understand that this is a particularly personal issue for her due to her own childhood when it was the Federation who were seen as the occupiers by some of her fellow Illyrians. And yet, there’s little here that makes me feel much for Una’s current (or past) situation.

Indeed, it’s Olusanmokun’s M'Benga who once again steals the show, even though he’s depicted here as more of an advisor to both Una and Uhura rather than given his own plotline. The idea of the kindly physician who is also a skilled warrior and an adept spy is so darned cool as the good doctor counsels the young Uhura in how to navigate this strange (new) world while also reminding Una that she can’t let her responsibility to the resistance movement overtake her oath to Starfleet. He even gets the best line of the hour: “My calling is medicine, healing people. It's the great mystery of my life that some of my strongest skills lie in opposition to that calling.”

The B story involves Christina Chong’s La’an, who’s been flirting with going over to the dark side all season, obsessing over what she thinks might be clues that there’s a traitor onboard the Enterprise. The thing is, nobody else buys her theories, not even her friend-with-benefits-but-actually-her-boyfriend Spock (Ethan Peck). Again, it’s a fairly low-impact plotline that culminates in the revelation that, whew, La’an is not crazy, but also, whoa, she just lied to Captain Pike (Anson Mount) to cover up the truth. Pike seems to maybe know there’s more going on here, and trusts La’an to do the right thing, but still…

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

So if Una’s next step up the promotion ladder is captain, how long until she gets her own ship and leaves the Enterprise for good? (Never to be mentioned or seen again, by the way.)

In her opening log, Una says that they’re at risk of “re-starting a very Cold War,” but shouldn’t that be “re-starting a shooting war”? The Klingons and the Federation are in a state of Cold War by the time Kirk is in command of the Enterprise, and presumably that’s been the situation since the end of the war depicted in Star Trek: Discovery …

The chief Klingon here is Kor, who I guess is supposed to be the Kor from The Original Series and Deep Space Nine who was played by the late, great John Colicos. Fine, I guess? (The House of Kor was also depicted in Star Trek: Discovery, although Kor himself was not.)

Speaking of Discovery, the shuttle Una and the gang take in this episode is the Cervantes, which according to Memory Alpha is a Stamets-type vessel. It’s gotta be named after either the Discovery’s Paul Stamets (who is considered lost and MIA at this point in the timeline) or possibly the real-life mycologist Paul Stamets who the character is named after. Right?

articles.title: The Corvette Grand Sport X delivers Porsche 911 performance for a fraction of the price
articles.summary: The Corvette Grand Sport X can help heal our automotive differences with its power and performance.
articles.body: My drive of the 2027 Corvette Grand Sport X began under oily black clouds, a torrential weather front releasing its grip on Manhattan — an inauspicious start for any mega-powered sports car. Rain pelted the waterlogged pavement, as I set course for the mountain-man roads of the Catskills, then on to Long Island and New England over three days. Fortunately, this Grand Sport, a name synonymous with value among Corvette fans, was the first of its kind: A 721-horsepower super-hybrid with a brainy, confidence-boosting AWD system. I popped the Corvette into Sport mode, Wet mode be damned. Finding tire grip galore on the Palisades Parkway, I realized the “X” badge on those wide flanks had changed the forecast to “fun.”  As a track-centric mid-engine sports car, the 2027 Corvette Grand Sport X is hardly representative of mass-market transportation. But the GSX still has something hopeful to say — or shout, with every seismic blast of its new LS6 V-8 engine — about the world’s renewed love affair with hybrids.  People have always made a statement about who they are, or the person they want to be, through the car they drive or the one they dream of owning. Beetle or BMW, Porsche or pickup, Stingray or Subaru. These choices are more fraught than ever as a zero-sum game emerges between EVs and internal combustion engine cars.  You can watch that standoff unfold on YouTube, with drag races between Teslas and seemingly every ICE car since the Model T. When I came of age in Detroit, true sports-car fans scoffed at such reductive straight-line contests, the equivalent of an arm-wrestling match to determine the most gifted athlete.  On a broader level, it doesn’t have to be this way. Electrified cars like the Grand Sport X can help change the conversation and build common ground on today’s scorched earth. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The Corvette’s sophisticated algorithms bring two often-warring tribes together. There’s electric business in the front, and a gasoline party in the back, with no physical connection between the electrified front axle and petroleum-powered rear wheels. Finely coordinated teamwork and integration makes the GSX the latest all-wheel-drive hybrid sports car that feels like an unfair fight against purely gasoline models.  GM could use some teamwork on the hybrid front. The company currently has just two gas-electric models. Both are Corvettes. Both use electricity strictly to boost performance, like a hybrid F1 racer, with fuel economy not part of the brief. In America, only hybrids have gained powertrain market share in 2026, with both EVs and pure ICE losing ground. With a record 15.4 percent of the market through June, hybrids are outselling EVs by nearly three to one. Even in China, hybrid sales are growing faster than those of EVs. Three companies, Toyota, Hyundai and Honda, now control 90 percent of this booming US hybrid market. Toyota and Lexus alone sold 600,000 hybrids through June. The windfall has seen Hyundai and Kia post their best overall sales in history, including a 115-percent jump for Kia’s growing hybrid lineup. Caught flatfooted after having gone all-in on EVs, GM is racing to bring fuel-saving plug-in hybrids back to its showrooms, supposedly beginning next year.  The GSX itself replaces the Corvette E-Ray, Chevrolet’s first hybrid sports car. But it’s an entirely different animal. The 650-horsepower E-Ray was a versatile grand tourer: fast and fluid, but a bit of a mellow yacht rocker. The GSX was expressly designed as a track assassin, with heightened power, roadholding, braking, and agility.  What GM engineers call the “baby ZR1X” adopts its electrified front axle directly from the 1,250-horsepower, 233-mph record setter that I tested at Sonoma Raceway. Most every internal part number is identical. But in keeping with the Grand Sport’s reputation as a sweet spot in the Corvette lineup, the GSX coupe’s $112,195 base price is less than half that of a ZR1X at $227,395. For 2027, a non-hybrid, 535-horsepower Grand Sport asks $88,495. That rear-wheel-drive Grand Sport will be more than enough for many buyers.  [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Some want more. So the GSX’s  721 horsepower represents a 186-hp bump over a Grand Sport or 2027 Stingray. Add a monumental 655 pound-feet of torque, and the GSX easily tops the 690 horses and 531 pound-feet of a McLaren Artura, a hybrid that starts from around $260,000. As in the ZR1X, the internal bearings in the electric motor were beefed up to handle a higher output of 186 horsepower and 145 pound-feet of torque. Push the GSX’s start button, and the engine crackles to life, before settling into a menacing basso idle. Floor the accelerator, and the  cabin fills with enough pummeling, martial sound to backdrop a Christopher Nolan epic. The electric motor plays its own whirring part, including a metallic overlay of selected frequencies amplified through the audio system. EV backers may believe silence is golden (sometimes it is) and scoff over ICE fans’ unwillingness to give up their thrashing cylinders. What they forget is that an engine’s sound offers not just drama and engagement, but critical somatic cues as to how fast you’re going, and a car’s gear or limits at a given moment. Yes, an EV can digitally imitate those cues. But for now, as with certain music, analog still beats digital among the performance cognoscenti. An optional performance exhaust for $1,995 is a worthy upgrade. Corvette engineers lavished attention on the center-mounted exhaust and its four trumpeting outlets to coax out its most-pleasing harmonic frequencies. Another $2,995 for a front-end lift system is another practical spend, to avoid scraping the low-slung front splitter on every steep driveway.  Displacing 409 cubic inches, the stroked V-8 coincidentally harkens to a bygone age of muscle, when Brian Wilson ticked off the Chevrolet Impala SS’s technical virtues in the Beach Boys’ hit “409.” (Hey, it was the ’60s).  Here in 2026, the LS6 makes that old 409 seem primeval, in tech, power, or efficiency. Pricey forged cylinders can deactivate to save fuel. A lofty 13:1 compression ratio is the stuff of race cars and also contributes to cleaner fuel burn. The engine reduces emissions by 28 percent versus its less-powerful predecessor.  [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The engine’s 520 pound-feet of torque sets a high for any naturally aspirated V-8 in production-car history. This overachiever also becomes the standard power plant in a 2027 Stingray, making this “basic” Corvette even more of a sports-car bargain at $73,495. The engine manages a 25-mpg highway rating, impressive for a Stingray that can nip 200 mph.  As noted, neither the GSX nor the ZR1X gives a hoot about fuel economy. Their adrenalized performance encourages its pilots to feel the same. The GSX topped out at 22 mpg during my drives. It settled in around 15 mpg, and dipped as low as 11 or 12 mpg during barnstorming runs through the Catskills. Whichever automaker can bring a two-seat, truly mass-produced electric sports car to market — whether Porsche or someone else — energy savings will be an easy win for Team Electric. The Corvette’s electric machine is fed by a tiny 1.9-kilowatt-hour battery mounted in the chassis’ spine, between driver and passenger. Again, that battery isn’t about efficiency or solo electric propulsion. Instead, its cells are designed to absorb regenerative energy like a fast-acting sponge, and spit it back out in rapid bursts. The motor fills any gaps in the engine’s output with an unbroken wave of torque, including during paddled upshifts from the eight-speed, dual-clutch automated gearbox.  Chevy cites a launch-controlled run to 60 mph in a sparkling 2.4 seconds, and a quarter-mile in 10.4 seconds at 131 mph. I manage 2.6 seconds to 60 mph, even on lumpy backroads in upstate New York. Those official measures are 0.1-seconds quicker than an E-Ray on both counts, and 0.2 seconds quicker than another track-centric Corvette: the mighty Z06 and its Ferrari-esque, flat-crankshaft V-8. As you’d expect, launch starts are less dramatic than in rear-drive Corvettes, all four tires hooking up with a yawn before you’re hammered into body-hugging bucket seats.  Familiar hardware, including a limited-slip rear differential with selectable Performance Traction Management settings, is retuned for this application. A superlative MagneRide suspension reads the road 1,000 times per second to adjust the viscosity of its magnetic-fluid dampers, and stiffen or soften shocks at individual wheels. The ride is firm but not spine-crunching, especially in Touring mode. Algorithms help dial in electric power for any situation, striving for handling balance and linear power delivery. In familiar tuning disagreements between passionate engineers, every GSX tiebreaker went to the track.  As compared to the E-Ray, “we’re keeping the edgier scenarios where the car feels more ready to pounce, versus a more-docile character,” says Keith Badgley, lead development engineer. [Image: The author’s gray tester. Stated simply, electrified front wheels take a major burden off of rear tires, here shod with Michelin Pilot Sport all-season tires in a fat 345/25/ZR21 size. Powerful carbon-ceramic brakes are standard, helping to explain a somewhat eye-opening $23,700 price jump from a standard Grand Sport. Like its ZR1X daddy, the GSX lets me brake deep into corners and jump back on throttle earlier, with fewer worries about the back end getting loose. In the rolling twisties of the Catskills, the GSX felt thrillingly athletic and on-its-toes. Hard-working front wheels palpably yank the ’Vette out of fast corners. Common sense is the only thing that will stop you.  The GSX also adopts the ZR1X’s specialized performance strategies. Hitting a “Charge +” button summons an Endurance mode, ensuring electrified wheels can deliver a consistent AWD jolt over a full tank of fuel, even during track sessions. A Qualifying mode preps the car for the fastest possible lap. Push-to-pass mode offers the full monty of gasoline and electric power on demand. To keep peace with neighbors, a Stealth mode lets the Corvette roll on electric power alone at speeds up to 50 mph.  The energy strategies make it virtually impossible to run the battery below 40 or 50 percent on public roads, no matter how hard you try. Selecting Charge + will also refill the battery over five miles or less of driving, using the gasoline engine and kinetic energy to generate electricity via the motor. Did I mention this Grand Sport makes a great first impression? Rolling into fabled Woodstock, the GSX underscored how the eighth-generation Corvette is (finally) widening its appeal beyond a traditional Boomer, rock n roll audience. I can still quibble with aspects of the C8 design, especially that bluff back end. But the Grand Sports’ 3.6-inch-wider chassis, cavernous side air inlets, and forged aluminum wheels add to its exotic supercar vibe. Everywhere I rolled up in the glowering gray GSX, someone would stop in their tracks to offer questions or compliments. And not just car fans, but people who didn’t always realize this was a Corvette, but were visibly impressed when they found out. Serious fans will recognize a Grand Sport’s traditional hash marks on rear fenders, rendered in classic Admiral Blue on my test car. The Corvette’s reworked interior will also win friends. A new auxiliary screen sits just left of the steering wheel, for easier access to launch control and PTM settings. There’s an intuitive Google-based infotainment system, graphical performance readouts, and the ingenious camera-based Performance Data Recorder to record and analyze track laps using telemetry software. A removable hardtop remains a signature coupe feature, and a GSX convertible starts from $119,195. My GSX coupe started from $122,845 at its richest 3LT trim level. A schmear of options lifted that to $140,080. By old measures, that’s a lot of money for a Corvette. But a Porsche 911 Carrera 4 GTS hybrid, with 189 fewer horsepower, starts from $191,650, and soars past $220,000 with a modest sprinkling of options. And again, the GSX costs roughly half the price of a ZR1X.  From the chip-on-shoulder Corvette to Porsche, Ferrari, Lamborghini and McLaren, buyers who might be ambivalent about EVs are warming to this new breed of hybrid sports cars. Their advantages are becoming harder to resist. For any type of car or SUV, I’ll argue that the hybrid love affair, rather than being seen as a rejection of EVs, is exactly the opposite. It’s a sign that Americans are already willing to meet electrification halfway. The next step becomes that much easier.

articles.title: A Court of Thorns and Roses Is Getting an Original Strategy Board Game, and Preorders Are Live
articles.summary: Take romantasy to the tabletop and fight for favor across the Courts of Prythian.
articles.body:
October is going to be a busy month for A Court of Thorns and Roses fans. The highly anticipated sixth book in the series from Sarah J. Maas is coming out on the 27th, but we're also getting two board games based on the beloved romantasy novel in the weeks before.

A Court of Thorns and Roses - Fate & Favor , from the minds at Goliath Games, is a new strategy board game where 1-7 players fight for power in the fae realm of Prythian. It’s up for preorder at Target for $24.99, with a release date set for October 11th. An ACOTAR Edition of Monopoly , listed for $39.99, is also coming out on October 1.

ACOTAR - Fate & Favor Board Game Now Up for Preorder

A Court of Thorns and Roses - Fate & Favor Board Game

This isn’t the first time we’ve seen a romantasy series get the board game treatment. In fact, Rebecca Yarros' Empyrean series has inspired Fourth Wing versions of Monopoly and Priorities . Instead of being a themed version of an existing game, however, this specific ACOTAR board game is entirely its own thing.

A Court of Thorns and Roses - Fate & Favor is full of familiar places and faces from the book. You play as one of the High Lords or Ladies of the seven Courts of Prythian: Night, Day, Dawn, Summer, Autumn, Winter, and Spring. You will forge alliances from this position, but loyalties can change as you ultimately compete for the most influence over the courts. It’s all about forging your own story and shaping your destiny through character abilities, court powers, event cards, and shifting fate tokens.

Created by genuine fans of the ACOTAR series, incredible detail has been poured into both the gameplay and artwork of Fate & Favor. It looks like tons of fun for fans of the books, but should also be enjoyable for those who haven’t had a chance to delve into this magical world. However, like the books, Fate & Favor is best-suited for ages 14+.

A special “Bookseller Variant” with exclusive packaging will be available at select bookstores in addition to the standard editions that's already up for preorder online. The contents of both editions will be the same.

Monopoly: A Court of Thorns and Roses Special Edition Board Game

Monopoly: A Court of Thorns and Roses Edition Board Game for Adults

As mentioned, ACOTAR is also getting a Monopoly Edition. Several, in fact. There's an Amazon-exclusive green variant , along with the classic red that matches the cover of the first book.

In both versions, the board highlights places from the series rather than your typical locations like Park Place and Boardwalk. It also features golden tokens with items from the book, including Feyre's Bow. Plus, the game offers manors and palaces over houses and hotels.

Preorders for the sixth and seventh A Court of Thorns and Roses books are also available. While neither book has a title yet, book six is out October 27, and book seven drops shortly after on January 12, 2027. Not much is known about the plot, either, but Maas claims the story is “big – really, really, really big."

Danielle is a Tech freelance writer based in Los Angeles who spends her free time creating videos and geeking out over music history.
