articles.title: You can now just point at a mess and this robot vacuum will suck it up
articles.summary: A free update brings on-device gesture control and a Gemini-powered voice assistant to the WALL-E-style robot vacuum
articles.body: Matic, my current favorite robot vacuum, just got a big upgrade. The company has launched Matic Cues, which brings voice and gesture control to the robot. Now, you can talk directly to your vacuum to tell it what you want it to do, or just point at a mess to have it spot-clean.  The feature launches today, August 13 at 2 pm ET, and will show as an option in the Matic app under Settings > Matic Cues. The update arrives just ahead of a planned price hike on September 9, which will see the WALL-E-style robot’s price go from $1,245 to $1,495. I’ve been playing with Matic Cues for a day or so, and so far it’s working well. Gesture control is the standout feature here, as it’s something no other robot vacuum offers — the company’s founders are both computer vision engineers who worked at Google Nest cameras, and have been developing the feature since 2017.  [Video: Testing Matic Cues gesture control] It works by waking up the robot with the wake word “Hey, Matic,” then waiting for it to “see” me (by turning toward my voice). I then point to the mess, say “clean here,” and off it goes. I did notice that if I wanted it to target a smaller area, I needed to crouch down to point at it. If I gestured from standing height, it cleaned a wider area, taking longer. It can also follow me, so saying “Hey Matic, follow me,” walking to and pointing at the mess, started a clean-up.  Because it uses the robot’s existing vision hardware — which includes five cameras — gesture control works entirely on-device and is coming to all existing Matic robots. While most robot vacuums let you spot-clean by drawing a zone in the app, I’ve found that method to be imprecise and not useful for quick cleanups. Some can also respond to a “clean here” voice command, but that’s based on the general area where you’re standing; Matic’s gesture-based implementation feels more focused.  [Image: The new built-in voice assistant also worked smoothly in initial testing. Voice control isn’t new on robot vacuums — nearly all work with Alexa and Google and some with Apple’s Siri, and many now have their own onboard voice assistants — including Roborock, Ecovacs, and Narwal. I’ve had mixed success with these long-term. Most require remembering exact commands; while “vacuum the kitchen” is easy to remember, other phrases are less intuitive and less flexible than Matic’s offering.  Matic uses the Gemini API to understand natural language, including commands like “vacuum the inside of the carpet” (thus avoiding the tassels), “clean just the hard floors,” and “clean the toekicks in the kitchen” — something I always want done right after cooking dinner. [Image: The voice assistant can understand natural language; instead of telling it “Return to dock,” you can just tell it to ”Go away.“ The robot could hear me from a room away and responded promptly — although it took a beat to go off and execute the command. It also doesn’t talk back; instead, its small display indicates it heard you and tells you what it’s doing. I was impressed how many commands it understood, including chained commands, like “clean the kitchen, vacuum the living room, and then mop the bathroom.” It also slunk back to its dock when I said, “Hey Matic, go away.” Handy if it’s underfoot when I’m cooking.  [Image: The voice assistant doesn’t talk back; it displays its confirmation of your command on its screen. One of Matic’s biggest selling points is that it doesn’t require the cloud and can be used without an internet connection. However, voice control does need both of those. While the company says the “Hey Matic” wake word is processed on-device, meaning no ambient chatter is sent to the cloud, any command after is sent to the Gemini API. A short chime tells you when anything is leaving the device. Mehul Nariyawala, cofounder and president of Matic, says the commands it sends are anonymized, adding that Matic chose cloud processing to support more than 75 languages and a wider variety of commands. The company plans to take the top 20 or 30 most-used commands and bring those locally in the future. Matic Cues is opt in, and you can turn it and the microphones off in settings. The trade-off between more convenience and more privacy is a constant tussle in the smart home. Roborock’s “Hey Rocky” voice assistant is entirely on device, but I rarely use it because it’s just not intuitive. So far I’ve found myself using “Hey Matic” much more frequently, as it’s just easier to talk to. The gesture control also solves a pain point I’ve long struggled with — getting a robot to clean the exact spot I want. For Matic users, this is a worthwhile update, and for those considering pulling the trigger, it’s a new convenience that makes a very good robot vacuum even better. Photos and video by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Diplomacy: The Golden Blade Is a Slimmed-Down, Card-Based Take on a Classic Strategy Board Game
articles.summary: Diplomacy: The Golden Blade is a card game that slims down and shortens the gameplay of the original Diplomacy board game, but it's not necessarily the better for it.
articles.body:
There are few more storied titles in the annals of board gaming than Allan B. Calhamer’s Diplomacy. Reputedly the favorite game of John F. Kennedy and Henry Kissinger, it sees players taking control of one of the great powers of Europe on a map of the continent and fighting it out for military supremacy. Its genius is a 1:1 combat system where pieces simply eliminate other pieces, making it impossible to gain an edge over rivals without an alliance. And it’s in these negotiations and inevitable betrayals that the thrill of the game lies.

The trouble with Diplomacy is that it runs long: with the optimal full complement of seven players, it can easily take up most of a day. Diplomacy: The Golden Blade makes the unlikely claim of retaining all the stab-in-the-dark charm of the original while cutting out the board and slashing the play time to around 15 minutes per player.

Without a board or unit pieces, there’s not a lot to talk about in terms of the box contents. Most of the components are cards, in two different sizes. The smaller ones are unit cards, representing your military forces. The larger ones are order cards that you’ll be playing to enact your decisions against opponents and these have both a picture and a text description of the order. There’s nothing special about the cards, artwork or icons, everything is clear and functional.

More curious of all are a series of punch-out cardboard tags that you use to delineate three rows and seven columns for your play area into which you place your unit cards. They show you what “level” you’ve reached in each row as you fill it with cards. These are fiddly, easily moved during play and, strictly speaking, unnecessary, although they do help all the players read the game state at a glance rather than card-counting.

Each player has a grid outlined by cardboard markers into which they play units cards from their hand. There’s a row for each of the three unit types: army, political and navy. One or two cards gives you level 1 in that unit type, three to six cards gives you level 2 and seven wins you the game. Most turns you’ll only get to play one card into your grid, although the randomly drawn selection in your hand may mean you can’t always play what you want.

However, this being diplomacy, these cards are tangential to the meat of the play, which is order cards. Every player gets an identical set of 12 of these, from which they’ll secretly select two each turn, one for each neighboring player. There are four kinds, one matching each type of unit which you can only choose if you have an equal or higher level in that unit type than that neighbor, and a fourth, “promises”, that you can play anywhere and which generally rely on your neighbor selecting a particular card.

In a turn, you’ll start by drawing a unit card, then there’s a timed five-minute negotiation period where you can make deals with other players – none of which are binding, of course. After that you play your order cards face-down before everyone reveals them all and you go around the table, working out the impact of each pairing. Finally, everyone plays a new unit card to their grid. It’s a simple core loop, easily taught, but the complexity is in the text on the order cards themselves.

Each kind has the potential to achieve different aims. Army orders let you interfere with your target’s units, allowing you to swap cards from your hand with theirs, or even removing played units from their grid. Political cards can give you a leg-up by letting you play an extra unit card or blocking enemy orders that interfere with the cards in your hand. Your naval choices include drawing extra cards, or blocking the most powerful army and political orders. This, then, is a cunningly varied game of rock, paper, scissors in which you get the chance to persuade your foes of your intentions, honorable or otherwise, before selecting an option.

However, it’s the promise cards that really give the game its flavor. Two of them, coalition and accord, give both players vital benefits if they both select a matching card. The former lets you block the order of your other neighbor, while the latter gives you two extra unit cards to draw. Alliance, on the other hand, allows that neighbor to resolve their chosen order against your other neighbor, and it can never be blocked. Critically the card says “may” ... so it leaves you very vulnerable to a sudden stab in the back.

Because you can’t play orders on an opponent unless you match or exceed their level in the matching unit type, players are caught between wanting to try and race towards the seven units needed to win and diversifying to protect themselves. Sometimes that decision is made for you by a lack of unit cards of the desired type, others by what your neighbors are choosing to collect. Either way, picking what to play each turn can be made part of both your ongoing strategy and your ongoing negotiations, bluffing about what you’re holding and might choose to play.

This network of options is, frankly, brilliant. Although it’s initially overwhelming, when you understand the effects of each card you’ll see how they interlock to create a framework of delineated decisions that feel like the free form of maneuvering and fighting in a map. Just like full-fat Diplomacy you can make and break alliances, broker deals, lie, cheat, and backstab to your heart’s content. And because your unit cards are visible to everyone, also just like classic Diplomacy, you’ll certainly have to betray one or both of your neighbors in order to win, because once you reach five or six units cards in a row, everyone will band together to stop you.

So it’s kind of a shame that, while you can still do all the things that drive the original game in this slimmed-down version, it turns out that the real draw of that game is in the cream that’s been lost.

It turns out that racing to seven cards simply isn’t enough time to establish the interpersonal relationships with the other players to really make it feel worthwhile. And it doesn’t matter if your opponents are friends or strangers: you still need time to build up a sense of trust, or develop a really festering feud, within the context of a single game. Without that, the inevitable twists of the knife just aren’t as painful, or as satisfying. Often, in games, the epic feel that players long for can only be delivered by devoting epic amounts of play time to deliver it.

Also, because the game is so short, and there’s a tendency for some players to race ahead in their favored unit type, it’s often a good idea to start getting those stabs in early. Accord is powerful if you pull it off because a bigger selection of cards means it’s more likely you’ll have what you need to push towards your goal. And everyone knows it, so you tend to get a round or two of that before such niceties give way to brutal warfare. Things pick up again towards the end of the game where alliance cards, suggested in the spirit of stopping the leader from getting over the line, can be exploited to give the betrayer a quick leg-up, but backstabbing is so commonplace at this point that it’s rarely the surprise it should be.

articles.title: Satechi’s New Six-Port USB-C Desktop Charger Offers 240W of Power
articles.body:
Satechi has released the ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger , a compact desktop charging brick with six USB-C ports that outputs enough power to keep your favorite power-hungry handheld gaming PC , gaming laptop , smartphone , and more topped up all at once. It even has a screen for those who want to see just how much their gear is drawing.

That 240W is a measure of the device’s total output, not any one USB-C outlet, but Satechi’s new charger can still push out 140W from either of its first two front-facing ports. That’ll charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full speed and is more than enough to max out the capacity of any handheld gaming PC you throw at it. The 240W Desktop Charger can also offer up to 100W on its second two ports, and up to 30W on the last two. Altogether, it has more ports and faster charging than most of IGN's current favorite USB-C chargers, both in general and for specific devices like the Steam Deck .

Satechi says its display can show the real-time power draw from each port, and that the charger “auto-detects each device’s requirements and balances output across active ports, keeping everything charged efficiently, quietly, and without overheating.” The product comes with a stand that lets you both rest the Desktop Charger horizontally or vertically, with a slight tilt so it’s easier to see the display. The charger comes in one color, Space Black.

The ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger costs $150 and is available now at Satechi’s website and Amazon .

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

articles.title: The MSI Claw EX is the most important PC handheld since Steam Deck — I still wouldn’t buy one
articles.summary: We review the MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus, a portable PC with Intel’s first dedicated handheld chip. It’s the most powerful truly portable handheld with the best battery life, but trips over certain games and costs far too much amidst RAMageddon.
articles.body: As The Verge’s resident handheld reviewer, I have nearly every portable gaming PC on a shelf in my house. The MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus is now the first one I reach for. Thanks to a next-gen Intel chip and improved MSI design, the Claw EX is the most powerful handheld that truly feels portable. It’s the handheld with the longest battery life, and the first Windows handheld I can trust to sleep and wake reliably.  Like the Steam Deck, when I press the power button, my game is always right where I left off. Unlike the Steam Deck, it can hibernate for days without losing a significant amount of charge.  Performance and battery? Windows and sleep? I wish I could say “you can have your cake and eat it too.” But you can’t. You probably shouldn’t. You can’t because this is a Ferris Bueller Product Review — this handheld costs a staggering $1,800, and you’ll be lucky to find it even at that price. (MSI’s Anne Lee tells me the US should have limited supply sometime this month.) Even if you could, you probably shouldn’t because Intel and MSI and Microsoft didn’t fully stick the landing. This is indeed a milestone for the handheld gaming space. But like actual milestones on a highway, you should probably drive right past. [Product: MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus | The Claw EX does have comfortable grips, I’ll give it that. Those manta-ray-wings wonderfully spread out its weight, to the point that the 1.73-pound (785g) portable feels far more comfortable than the 1.58-pound (715g) Xbox Ally X when I hold it above me in bed. And while a $1,800 handheld should really have an amazing OLED screen, I definitely prefer the Claw EX’s 8-inch 1920 x 1200 48-120Hz VRR screen to the comparatively cramped 7-inch 1080p one in the Allys. The only real problem is glare — the ultra-glossy screen was not great on my road trip this summer. But the controls are merely average, the fan is loud (though it’s whoosh not whine), and those manta-ray grips can buzz my hands when I turn up the speakers. Sound reverberates inside. [Image: I love the grips. Buttons are fine. The joysticks are drift-resistant magnetic ones, but really need tuning. I undershoot and overshoot too much. [Image: Here’s the underside of those meaty grips. I’d prefer grippier, but the stippling is not bad at all. No, the Claw EX’s true strengths are performance and battery — but even there, the handheld sometimes let me down. I’ve always loved the phrase “potato graphics.” It’s such a fun way to describe what games look like when your rig is too weak. They’re rough and pasty — like a potato! — even when running smoothly. Or if you turn up the graphics anyway, you get a “slideshow” because your hardware can’t deliver enough frames. The first reason I reach for the Claw EX, before any other handheld, is because I don’t automatically get potatoes or slideshow when I fire up demanding PC games. Like my colleague Jay Peters showed you on launch day, the Claw EX makes games look so much sharper than they do on a Steam Deck, and it’s not just the Deck that’s getting beat. The Xbox Ally X with its AMD Z2 Extreme chip, and the old MSI Claw 8 with Intel Lunar Lake, aren’t playing demanding games smoothly at the 1080p or 1200p resolution of their screens. The Claw EX often can, and I’m seeing around 40 percent more performance than the Xbox Ally X in my tests at 1080p. In many games, like Forza Horizon 6 and Cyberpunk 2077, that’s the difference between playing at native resolution or settling for less. [Table: 1080p benchmarks] When I add a little upscaling, I can even start enjoying games I haven’t been able to enjoy handheld because of potato graphics. I could swing lightsabers in Star Wars Jedi: Survivor and crack whips in Indiana Jones and the Great Circle at good quality with smooth frame rate while binging K-dramas with my spouse. Until, suddenly, I couldn’t — seemingly because Intel’s drivers aren’t playing nice with some games yet. When my Indy visited the Great Pyramid, the Intel chip would simply not run at the wattage I set, and I found spots where the entire game would repeatedly freeze or even trigger a full system hang. In Jedi: Survivor, the game is weirdly stuttery in some areas, even though I get far more resolution and smoother frame rate on the Claw EX than the Xbox Ally X. Until a recent Intel update, Expedition 33 had what looked like intense graphical corruption around its particle effects in the game, turning them into glitchy spots of light. [Table: 720p benchmarks] And you should take Returnal benchmark numbers with a grain of salt, because many graphical effects are entirely missing on Intel. Undergrowth and volumetric fog are barely there; stone objects no longer explode into showers of rock; transparent energy shields are weirdly opaque. The second reason I reach for the Claw EX is that battery life. Like some of its competitors, it has a big 80 watt-hour pack — but the Intel chip can stretch that battery even further than the competition. Take Cyberpunk 2077, for example. To hit a smooth 70fps average at 720p resolution, the Xbox Ally X and the last-gen Claw require around 30 watts of total power, draining their batteries in roughly 2.5 hours. With the new Claw, you can reach that same performance with 21 watts, giving you a whole extra hour on a charge. [Table: Battery life vs. performance] Or take Balatro, the 2D magic poker game that’s become my best-case battery life test. Just by toggling the Claw EX’s “Endurance” mode and setting the screen to 48Hz instead of 120Hz in the Quick Settings menu, I got the handheld’s total system power draw down to just 6.5 watts, enough to last 12 whole hours on a charge. It’s rare to get epic battery life for 2D indie games and performance for triple-A ones from a single chip. But this strength of the Claw EX is flawed, too. When I drain the battery below 15 percent charge with triple-A games, performance dramatically dips. My chip couldn’t maintain its 25W performance mode and switched to 15W instead. That performance didn’t immediately come back when I plugged the handheld in. [Image: Friends don’t let friends run lightweight games at 120Hz. At 48Hz, you can play this same game five hours longer on a charge. And though the Claw EX might be the first Windows handheld that properly sleeps and wakes right out of the box, that doesn’t excuse its other Windows woes. I can’t count the number of times I’ve launched a game and been left staring at a black screen, wondering when it’ll finally appear, only to discover it was already running in the background and didn’t show itself. I don’t appreciate having to hold down the Task Switcher button to fix a game that didn’t properly launch full-screen, or having to quit out to desktop mode to download the latest Intel drivers. The handheld should really automatically alert me when they’re available. [Image: MSI’s “AI Engine” setting does seem slightly smarter. It’ll generally run games at 25W TDP, but I see it ramping up when loading and downloading to make wait times shorter. I nearly did a spit take when Windows told me I couldn’t use my handheld’s control panel because, and I quote, “Most of the features in Quick Settings require administration privileges. To use all the features, please switch to an administrator account.” Thankfully, a reboot fixed that. I instinctively reach for the Claw EX, instead of any other handheld, because I’m borrowing it from Intel instead of paying cash — and because I’m willing to tolerate its idiosyncrasies for fewer potato graphics. At $1,800, I wouldn’t. Photography by Sean Hollister / The Verge

articles.title: CMF’s clip earbuds hit the balance between cheap and good
articles.summary: ﻿The CMF Clip Pro are a very comfortable option for those that hate things in their ears.
articles.body: Clip earbuds are an exercise in compromise. It’s an inherent aspect of their design — and physics. They can be more comfortable for people that don’t like something jammed in their ear, but sound response suffers. Ambient awareness is great because you can easily hear the sound around you, which means to hear your own music the buds need to be turned up and potentially leak sound out to your neighbors. For what they offer, they can also get pricey, with popular pairs from Bose, Sony, and Shokz reaching $200. The CMF Clip Pro, though, are under $100, and while they still have those compromises, they handle them well. [Product: CMF Clip Pro | CMF is Nothing’s budget sub-brand, and because it tends to release earbuds in the $40–$60 range, I was expecting the same when I first heard about the Clip Pro. But instead, the Clip Pro are $99 — the same price as Nothing’s Ear 3A that just came out last month with more features (and also more issues). Only a few days after release and the Clip Pro are already on sale at $79, which puts them at the price I think they should be. [Image: Instead of being placed inside the ear canal, the Clip Pro’s speaker sits just outside it and a band wraps around the ear to keep them secure. Comfort is the Clip Pro’s big advantage. The flexible band avoids any pinching around the helix, and I didn’t experience any discomfort with how the speaker orb or battery/control capsule sat in and behind my ear. A clip design is the best option for those that have trouble fitting earbuds in their ear canals. Not having the sealed fit in your ear canals, though, affects the sound consistency, and I wouldn’t suggest doing any critical listening on the Clip Pro — or any clip earbuds, for that matter. Even so, the sound balance didn’t negatively affect my listening of my regular playlists and KCSN radio station app. By default, there’s a bass boost, which is necessary without a sealed fit but doesn’t cause the sound to be overly bassy (which other Nothing earbuds can be). There’s a three-band EQ in the Nothing X app to adjust to taste, although as with other Nothing earbuds and headphones, the EQ can be tricky to use. Increasing a slider doesn’t always boost that frequency band, but instead lowers the other frequencies (increasing the bass, for example, actually brings down the mids and highs). It takes some getting used to and extra finagling. The Clip Pro support fixed spatial audio, which adds more space to the sound (I didn’t find it objectionable, but preferred the sound without it), as well as high-res audio over LDAC. The differences with high-res on an open-ear design are so minute, it’s not worth it, especially with any ambient noise around. While listening to my radio app, the DJ’s voice could get difficult to understand during talk breaks with traffic going by. Boosting the volume can solve the problem, but it can also cause the sound to leak out to be heard by those close to you (benchmates on the bus or subway, for example). Turning on anti-leakage mode in the app cuts higher frequencies, but also adversely affects sound quality. The sound only leaks at high volumes, so it’s best to just turn them down. There are multiple options for adjusting the volume in those situations, including directly from your device, with buttons on the capsules that rest behind each ear, or with a dial on the case (assignable in the app). The dial is also a button that can play and pause, skip forward and back, or call up your phone’s assistant. [Image: The Clip Pro’s case has a dial that can control the volume and be used as a button. There isn’t quite enough resistance to the dial, so at times while the case was in my pocket, volume would go up or down by a click or two. I ended up disabling the dial and either using the buttons on the earbuds, which work well although with a slight delay, or just pulling out my phone instead of the case. And with functionality disabled the dial becomes a great fidget toy. The Clip Pro are pretty good with calls and don’t exhibit the buggy functionality I experienced with the Nothing Ear 3A, where the compression on my voice would drastically adjust based on the ambient sound when I started talking. The noise gate is still very aggressive to filter out any surrounding sound and can clip the very end of a word, but when I was speaking at normal volumes while walking down the street, my wife was able to understand me easily. Soft-spoken people might run into issues, though. When I spoke quietly, I sounded very muffled and it took her lots of concentration to try and figure out what I said. That call quality epitomizes the CMF Clip Pro, and it’s the same with their sound. The earbuds are good at what they do under the constraints of the technology. And their comfort, along with their price, make them great when you don’t want something deep in your ear. Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 2 – The Legacy Review
articles.summary: Grand Theft Auto 2 boasts a number of noticeable technical improvements over the original and feels far better to play, but I'm glad its odd and unrecognisable setting was a one-time experiment.
articles.body:
Over the next few months, I’m going to be taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t carry IGN’s typical score out of 10, because it really wouldn’t be at all fair to simply pick apart old games published multiple hardware generations ago and make them sweat under the harsher standards of 2026. What we will be doing, however, is re-examining what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release, digging into what they achieved and the legacies they established, and rediscovering how much fun each of them remain today. We’ll also be identifying both the parts of the GTA experience that have seen the most evolution and growth, as well as the parts that remain fascinating, commendable, and timelessly impressive. At the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly sit in my long-term love for this series.

Grand Theft Auto 2 arrived right at the tail end of the 20th century, sticking with the same brand of top-down turmoil that previously propelled its predecessor to great success. It’s a noticeable refinement of the original in some fundamental ways – slightly more forgiving thanks to the ability to save, and also a bit smoother to drive around in. It didn’t, however, replace its antiquated, tank-like on-foot controls for something that better exploited the dual-analogue controllers that had rapidly reinvented the status quo in the late ’90s. What it did shed was the original GTA’s recognisable, contemporary setting. It instead opted to set its action at an unspecified point in the near future, in a stylised, retro-futuristic backdrop called Anywhere City, USA – a place overrun by gangs, ruled by a megacorporation, and featuring the highest rate of Elvis Presley’s per capita this side of Graceland. Did it work? Well, the answer – unlike Anywhere City’s proliferation of Elvis impersonators – requires a little more conversation.

GTA 2 immediately comes off as a game with a bit of an identity crisis. Even if you ignore the fact that it sports a totally different look and vibe to the original, it also completely clashes with its own box art, and even its own intro movie – which features contemporaneous ’90s cars and an obvious New York setting. At the time of its release, I actually bounced off GTA 2 rather quickly, and this was absolutely a major reason. As soon as it began it just felt like an entirely unrelated product to everything that had come before – up to and including the tone-setting FMV intro it just served me. That’s a really weird problem to have. As a result, I don’t feel like I stuck around anywhere near long enough back in 1999 to get a feel for how much slicker it actually is to play.

Despite the fact it costs in-game currency to use, the addition of a save function represents a clear improvement over the original. Just head to the nearest church, and the good lord above will remember your progress for you. Jesus indeed saves in Anywhere City, albeit for a fee. Straight away GTA 2 appears a little more aware it’s a PC and home console product. By the late ’90s, hefty, mission-oriented action games had largely moved on from the ruthless arcade philosophy of starting from scratch every session with a tiny set of lives. Developer DMA Design adjusted its format accordingly, albeit only slightly. That is, GTA 2 retains score-based progression, still operates with strictly limited lives, and is hard as hell – but saving is nonetheless a crutch the original did not have.

A newly added health bar addresses another major frustration from the original GTA. If you’re trying to avoid cheating just to get through the missions, the boosted health is an even more useful fix than saving. Health in GTA 2 works on a 10-point scale (with five hearts that can be halved). This is in stark contrast to the first GTA, which essentially operates with your character on his or her final sliver of life at all times – where you’re instantly wasted after sustaining just a single hit. The tank controls make dodging incoming fire hideously difficult in both games, but the challenge is at least tempered here by the very sensible addition of that extra padding. It doesn’t make it easy, by any means, but it’s certainly less annoying.

The improvements don’t stop there. GTA 2’s camera is considerably less janky and, while it still shimmies around a little as you drive, it does a way better job of tracking cars smoothly. Cars also self-straighten when blazing along the streets, so it’s far less finicky to line up within a lane – or indeed change lanes – with less furious tapping of the d-pad.

There are also far fewer obstacles for cars to get hung up on than there were in the original. With the top-down perspective, it can be challenging to tell what objects are rooted into the ground and will cause a crash, because depth can be a difficult thing to effectively communicate from directly above. GTA 2 skirts this by having skinny things like light poles not even register to cars at all. It's not a particularly realistic approach, but it cuts down on the constant collisions which bogged down the pace of the original.

Cars can now be fitted out with weapons and gadgets, like machine guns, mines, and oil slick traps, and the amount of handheld weapons has been more than doubled. GTA 2 adds tossable explosives like grenades and Molotovs, a suppressed SMG that won’t alert other nearby NPCs, a shotgun for more devastating close quarters damage, dual pistols to dial up the John Woo factor, and a futuristic electro gun that will saute suckers into skeletons. The electro gun is particularly nifty considering it can lock onto multiple targets at once, but a mild auto-aim function (an assist sorely missed in GTA 1) makes for less frustrating combat all around, regardless of what weapon you’re using.

Despite the more polished gameplay, GTA 2 still leaves me indifferent in a number of ways. I know that merging the aesthetic of ’40s and ’50s vehicles with a crime-ridden, near-future corporate dystopia is a stylistic choice, but it just doesn’t really grab me. It’s not that I don’t find this era of automotive history interesting – I love skidding around in games like Mafia and LA Noire – but they just look silly in this setting and don’t sync with it at all.

It’s really easy to tell cars apart in the original GTA, because they resemble real cars and they all look quite distinct. In GTA 2, there are more than 60 different vehicles, but there are far too many that look too similar to each other – and none that really resemble anything particularly iconic. They just look like caricatures of cars, and I vastly prefer the realism of the original GTA’s vehicles.

I also prefer the original’s maps over the three districts of Anywhere City (the Downtown Sector, the Residential Sector, and the Industrial Sector). Now, GTA 2 boasts sharper graphics than its slightly murkier predecessor, and the effect of this cleaner image arguably makes it the more timeless-looking of the two. On PC there are even day and night versions of each area. However, with the possible exception of the Residential Sector (which is the most varied), there’s a plainness to Anywhere City that I don’t think the cities in the original GTA shared.

I do enjoy how much more alive and dangerous Anywhere City feels – with muggers, carjackers, and gang members scurrying the sidewalks everywhere as an omnipresent threat. However, I don’t think it has the charm of Liberty City, San Andreas, or Vice City – as primitive as their renditions were by modern standards.

I’m willing to concede my preference here may simply be because the amount of time I sunk into those maps dwarfs the moments I’ve spent in Anywhere City, but there is also something bigger at play. The 3,500 pound, 350-horsepower elephant in the room here is Driver, which was released on PlayStation in European territories about five months before GTA 2, in June 1999. Now, the original Driver has no on-foot component – so it’s not an entirely like-for-like comparison – but it is a fully 3D, open-world car chase classic that rapidly cemented itself as more or less my favourite game of all time at that moment. I’d seen the future, and GTA 2 couldn’t lure me back.

The dawn of 3D action-driving games was upon us. Prior to Driver we’d already seen Midtown Madness on PC, from future Midnight Club, Smuggler’s Run, and Red Dead Redemption developers Angel Studios. Following Driver came Mucky Foot’s ambitious but janky Urban Chaos in late 1999 on PC and early 2000 on PlayStation, which boasted a primitive brand of driving and third-person action. A PlayStation-exclusive Driver sequel followed in late 2000, where you could exit cars to steal another. June 2001’s World’s Scariest Police Chases sank with little trace after arriving on PS1 after the PS2 had launched, but it was actually a surprisingly decent open-world driving game of its own considering the totally outmoded hardware it was running on.

Any way you slice it, GTA 2 was a buck late and a dimension short to be a part of the first wave of 3D action-driving games.

Of course, the series wouldn’t be the bridesmaid for long – but that’s a discussion for next time.

Playing Grand Theft Auto 2 again in 2026, I’ve definitely found myself with a stronger appreciation for its technical improvements over the original. Certainly much greater than I gave it credit for back as a teenager in 1999. The driving is better, the shooting is better – and those are important and welcome gains. However, I just cannot muster any true enthusiasm for its retro-futuristic setting. I don’t know that I’d go so far as to call it aggravating but, in the words of the king of rock and roll, it just ain’t satisfactioning me.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: Lanterns Series Premiere Review: How HBO’s True Detective-Style Superhero Mystery Reinvigorates James Gunn's DCU
articles.summary: With a finely honed Dynamic Duo lighting the way, Lanterns serves as a critical return to form for the DCU in its first episode. Read our spoiler-free review.
articles.body:
This is a spoiler-free review of the first episode of Lanterns Season 1. The series debuts on HBO and HBO Max on Sunday, August 16.

It’s safe to say that a lot is riding on the first season of Lanterns . This is one of the first key pieces of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU that isn’t directly steered by Gunn himself. We’ve seen enough by now to know that Gunn himself has a solid handle on the DC brand. Creature Commandos, Superman, and Peacemaker have all been enjoyable. But can this fledgling cinematic universe thrive when he hands the reins over to other creators? Supergirl certainly calls that into question , casting doubt on Gunn’s lofty claims about strong scripts and clear artistic visions being the driving force of this line. The DCU needs a win right about now, and I’m happy to say that Lanterns is ready and able to deliver in its first episode.

Granted, it’s been tough to know what exactly to make of this series. For a franchise as fundamentally fantastical as this one, the prospect of focusing on an Earth-based murder mystery and downplaying the actual Green Lantern elements wasn’t necessarily appealing to all fans. The initial Lanterns trailer did little to assuage the fears of those concerned by that premise. And then co-creator Damon Lindelof really stepped in it with some of his comments, to the point where no less a DC authority than Grant Morrison felt compelled to clap back . Suffice it to say, DC and Warners didn’t really do themselves any favors with the marketing of Lanterns, but the proof is ultimately in the pudding.

Yes, Lanterns is essentially what the trailers and early previews have made it out to be. It’s as much a True Detective and Slow Horses-style murder mystery as it is a superhero drama (and, in fact, features veterans of both shows among its creative team). It’s not necessarily going to appeal to viewers intent on seeing the cosmic side of the Green Lantern mythos on full display. We rarely even see Kyle Chandler’s Hal Jordan put on the costume. And given how ugly and clunky this live-action rendition of the suit really is, that’s probably a good thing. The series generally looks good, but more in that quietly stylized, more grounded True Detective way than because of any budget-busting special effects. In short, Green Lantern purists who want unadulterated, comic book-accurate, ring-slinging cosmic spectacle are setting themselves up for disappointment with this show.

But for those willing to abandon preconceived notions and take Lanterns for what it is, this strange combination of superhero adventure and terrestrial murder mystery works surprisingly well. A lot of that comes down to the chemistry between Chandler’s Hal and his trainee, Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart. Hal has never been portrayed as the nicest or most well-adjusted member of the Justice League in various DC media, but here he’s downright hostile and standoffish to his young charge. As much as the first episode lays the foundation for an urgent investigation in the remote town of Rushville, Nebraska, it makes it clear that the real conflict is between Hal and John. One is a cocky, grizzled veteran suspicious that his space cop handlers are trying to replace him. The other is a former Marine with a deep desire for the ring but limited tolerance for shenanigans. To say the two butt heads in the first episode is putting it mildly indeed.

The series leans a lot on that core dynamic, making it crucial that it finds the right actors for the job. That’s one area where Lanterns succeeds unequivocally. Both actors are pitch-perfect in their portrayals of these iconic (if sometimes barely recognizable) characters. Chandler probably isn’t the first name to pop up on anyone’s list of dream Hal Jordan actors. He wasn’t even DC’s original choice for the part , it seems. And were the series striving for a more traditional, youthful take on the character, Chandler would obviously be a poor fit. But that’s not the goal here. This is a version of Hal who’s been active in the DCU for decades and truly feels the weight of those years. Chandler expertly captures that unique blend of exasperation, paranoia, and deep-seated overconfidence that define the DCU’s Hal Jordan. The last thing he feels like doing is training the guy who’s trying to steal his job, and he makes that clear in every interaction with John.

As for John, Pierre brings a quiet, no-nonsense charisma to the screen that contrasts nicely with Hal’s fiery bravado. John is quiet, composed, and stoic, qualities that could make for a very boring role in the wrong hands. Fortunately, Pierre is able to bring enough subtle nuance to the screen that his character never comes across as dull or underdeveloped. He’s reserved, but underneath it all he burns with desire. We see how badly he wants the ring, even if it means putting up with an endless stream of nonsense from his superior officer.

It’s also nice to see the first episode dig a little bit into the racial undertones of this Training Day-esque dynamic. In one scene, a seething John calls his father for advice and is reminded that white men like Hal Jordan have the privilege of being eccentric and difficult. Not so for a Black man trying to prove his worthiness for the most exclusive law enforcement gig in the entire universe. At least at this early stage, it doesn’t appear that Lanterns is going to be steeped in the racial tensions of modern America to the same degree that Lindelof’s previous DC series was , but it’s still satisfying to have that element acknowledged – especially given how important John Stewart was to the early diversification of DC’s comic book universe decades ago.

On the subject of John Stewart, Sr. (played as a young man by J. Alphonse Nicholson and an older man by Sherman Augustus), the premiere teases a very intriguing dynamic there that’s sure to be explored in future episodes. It’s such a common trope for superhero media to paint their protagonists as orphans yearning for a lost father figure. That’s even baked into Hal’s origin story. But Lanterns is clearly striving for something much different with John’s family background, adding in new layers and details that aren’t necessarily taken from the comics. It’s a useful reminder that while the series isn’t afraid to alter the source material in sometimes profound ways, those alterations are about more than simply making Green Lantern practical in a small-screen format.

Once the Hal/John dynamic is firmly established, the premiere sets about laying the groundwork for the murder mystery that looks to be fueling the conflict in Season 1. To be frank, said mystery isn’t the reason to tune into the series, at least at this early stage. It gets the job done in terms of moving the plot from A to B, but for now the conflict is pretty small in scope. It’s mostly about Hal’s uphill battle to convince everyone around him (John included) that the dead bodies in front of them have extraterrestrial ties.

Here again, the various characters and their interpersonal clashes are what make the series shine. Early in the episode, viewers are introduced to another major character in Kelly Macdonald’s Kerry, the no-nonsense sheriff in charge of keeping the peace in the formerly quiet town of Rushville. As much as Chandler and Pierre’s icy dynamic fuels the series in its first episode, there’s also plenty of fun to be had in the equally standoffish relationship between Hal and Sheriff Kerry. There’s all the bickering over jurisdiction and one-sided flirtation you’d expect. Kerry quickly develops into a very fun, likable character who’s every bit the effective foil to Hal that John is.

Rounding out the notable cast members introduced in Episode 1 are Garret Dillahunt as local cowboy/ranch tycoon William Macon and Poorna Jagannathan as another Rushville native named Zoe. Macon serves his purpose as a charming but quietly unsettling antagonist figure with murky ties to the town’s murder mystery. Zoe, meanwhile, quickly strikes up a close bond with John, allowing the series to explore shades of the character that aren’t possible through Hal alone. Rushville is a small town full of interesting personalities, offering plenty of room for growth in the coming seven episodes.

Again, the murder mystery itself gets the job done in terms of plot catalysts, but it’s the characters who tend to shine more than the plot in Episode 1. It is worth noting, however, that the premiere keeps one big reveal under its hat until the final moments. This twist is sure to be as controversial as anything the show has to offer in its debut chapter. But as far as throwing viewers off-guard and hinting at a larger, more ambitious scope for the series, it delivers just what’s needed. If the prospect of plainclothes Green Lanterns loudly squabbling and rubbing elbows with cowboys isn’t enough to lure you in, this twist might just do the trick.

articles.title: Wingspan Pocket Takes What Makes the Original Board Game Fun and Shrinks It Down into a Pocketable Card Game
articles.summary: It's striking how Wingspan Pocket successfully recreates the feel and basic strategies of the original board game, in a fraction of the complexity and play time.
articles.body:
You’ve probably heard of Wingspan , the multi-million selling game of bird ecology that introduced a whole new audience to the strategic delight of engine-building games . But however widely appealing the theme of the game might be, it presented a significant barrier to new players in the form of rules overhead. There’s a lot to learn in the game, and a lot more to master.

This new game, from Elizabeth Hargrave, the same designer as the original, aims to slash that barrier down by presenting many of the same mechanics in a convenient, bite-sized box. As we saw in our recent review of Diplomacy: The Golden Blade , however cleverly you cut down a game, there’s a risk you’ll lose what made it special.

Half of the box is taken up with a stash of resin eggs which will be instantly familiar to fans of the original game. These are all one base color but they compensate with a variety of freckles and speckles of pattern, making them look surprisingly realistic. Rooting around in the eggs, you’ll also find a packet of wooden feathers, one color for each player.

The other half is filled with cards. Mostly this is one giant deck of bird cards which will, again, look very familiar to Wingspan veterans, featuring a similar layout and, in many cases, the same bird with the same artwork, although the mechanical details are different. Some cards do have all-new art, and there are also some birds that are entirely new to this edition. Whatever the provenance, the bird pictures remain a delight, full of detail, life and movement.

In addition to the bird cards there are some player aids, a nest card for each player, and some smaller decks. One is an automaton for solo play , another, of smaller, fiddly cards, has a series of goals players try to complete during the game.

Cards in Wingspan Pocket are double-sided. On one side there’s a food symbol for things birds like to eat; on the other is a bird itself. Players get dealt six cards and get to decide which two of them they’re going to hold as birds, with the remainder being kept to play as food. The rest of the cards are divided into four and the top card flipped off each stack and kept face up. There’s thus a selection of four different birds and four possible foods to choose from.

Each player also gets a nest card with an egg token on it and the card details one of three actions they can take on their turn: play a bird from your hand, take cards, or place eggs. Each bird has a cost in specific foods and, sometimes, eggs as well, and you’ll need to have these available to pay if you want to take the first action, after which you lay the bird to the right of your nest. Otherwise, picking up cards lets you choose any two from the selection of food or birds as you like, while the egg action lets you place eggs on three different cards.

Most birds have some kind of special power which is often related to their real-life behavior or ecology. The nefarious common Cuckoo lets you place an egg on another of your birds. The ghostlike Snowy Owl lets you draw a bird at random and tuck it under the owl, becoming a prey item, if its wingspan is under 100cm. The extravagantly named Turquoise-Browed Motmot gives every player the chance to blind draw a food card. Once you have any birds in play you use a feather token on your turn, moving from your cards from left to right and instituting that effect in sequence. First the nest with its choice of actions, then each bird’s special power.

In this way you are essentially creating an engine, like a much simplified version of the three-habitat engines that characterize the original Wingspan. Once you have birds in play that provide food or eggs then you need to take those actions from your nest less often, meaning you can put birds into play faster. It’s an optimization exercise, but there’s a surprising amount of nuance from this simple setup. In your initial selection, for example, it’s helpful if you can have one of the birds you’ve kept provide a resource that helps you play the second. And it’s strangely satisfying when your bird line-up clicks into gear.

What you’re really aiming for is some kind of combo between the bird powers in your line up. The Kookaburra, for instance, lets you pick a fish or mouse food type for free so it combines brilliantly with the Inca Tern or Secretarybird which let you discard those food types respectively to gain two cards of your choice, meaning you’ll never have to waste nest actions taking cards again.

You can try and specialize in particular resources, or go for a broad base. And as your hand of available bird and food cards change, you’ll need to be constantly revisiting your strategies to keep things in line. Waiting to see if the food or birds you want to extend your strategy are going to be available in the selection when your turn rolls around is surprisingly exciting.

The game ends when one player gets six birds in their row, at which point you flip your nest card over and it becomes a handy track to tally your points. Each bird card has a points value printed on it, with more expensive or less useful birds being worth more points. You also get a point for each egg and each tucked card. In the advanced version of the game, which you’ll want to use after your initial grapple with the rules, there are also two goal cards in play which reward you with additional points for having eggs on birds that meet their printed criteria. Worth three or fewer points, say, or having a wingspan over 66cm. The whole game takes just 10-15 minutes per player.

Goal cards are important because they significantly enrich the strategic decisions in building your engine. Birds that meet one or both criteria are obviously more valuable and you have to balance the need to acquire and play them with the utility of special powers on birds that don’t fit the bill. Given that you only get six birds maximum in a game, the margins on these decisions can be wafer thin. It can also sometimes be frustratingly random if you just never get the chance to grab good or high-scoring birds when they’re available, or find complementary powers to create a good engine. Them’s the breaks, but it’s far less annoying in this half-hour package than it would be in a longer game.

If you’re familiar with the original, the truly striking thing about Wingspan Pocket is how successfully it recreates the feel and basic strategies of the original in a fraction of the complexity and play time. It’s a masterclass in trimming fat, from the clever way cards act as both food and birds, removing all the rules around the original’s food dice while retaining the seed or randomness, to the way birds synergize effectively in one row instead of three habitats. Sure it’s less strategic and skillful overall, but the improvement in convenience and accessibility is so huge that it’s easily a worthwhile price to pay.

articles.title: Upcoming Nintendo Switch 2 Games: Release Dates for 2026 and Beyond
articles.summary: Building up the Switch 2 library.
articles.body:
We now have our hands on the Nintendo Switch 2 , a new console from one of the biggest names in gaming. Alas, a new console is only as valuable as the library of games you can build on it.

Thankfully, Nintendo hasn't been shy about planned releases over the next year. In the second half of 2026, we'll be getting our hands on a mix of Switch 2 exclusives, third-party releases, and the benefit of backward compatibility with any games still launching on the original Switch. Without further ado, here are all of the new Switch 2 games we can look forward to in 2026 and beyond.

All Upcoming Switch 2 Games With Release Dates

Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition (August 28, 2026)

While we wait for more news about FromSoftware’s next game, The Duskbloods (which will be a Switch 2 exclusive), we finally know when the GOTY-winning masterpiece that is Elden Ring will be coming to the Nintendo console. The Tarnished Edition will include two new starting classes as well as new armor sets, all of which will also be available as an upgrade for folks who already own the game on PC or other consoles.

This one caught my attention from its first teaser, in large part because of the particularly clean retro anime art style. Orbitals is an intergalactic adventure built for co-op play in a seemingly similar vein to Hazelight Studios games like Split Fiction and It Takes Two. We were big fans in our hands-on preview !

It’s a classic. This year’s iteration of NBA 2K will launch on the Switch 2 at the same time it becomes playable on PC and other consoles. Each version of the game features a different cover athlete, either Victor Wembanyama ( Standard ), Derrick Rose ( Ultra ), and, for the first time ever, a WNBA player, Caitlin Clark ( Deluxe ).

RuneScape: Dragonwilds (September 15, 2026)

RuneScape got a bit of a makeover with this new open world crafting and survival game that was initially released last year, and is finally coming to Switch 2 this fall.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave (September 17, 2026)*

We finally have a release date for the next game in the Fire Emblem series, which already happens to be available to preorder . Here’s a snippet of what to expect from the official Nintendo listing : “Worthy fighters from all over the land have come to Dagsion, the capital city of the Dagdan Empire, to compete in the Heroic Games for the chance to win one wish. Among the combatants are four heroes tied to the fate of the world.” You can learn more about how the game balances those four heroes in our hands-on preview .

Trine 6: Together in Time (September 17, 2026)

If you’re looking for a cozy platformer you can play with a friend, Trine 6 might have you covered. The latest side-scrolling sequel from FrozenByte is designed with co-op in mind, so you can test your friendship on movement combos and puzzles.

Another Eden Begins (September 17, 2026)

From Masato Kato, the writer behind Chrono Trigger, comes Another Eden Begins, a completely fresh RPG that takes you on a journey across the past, present, and future. Recruit companions from a roster of 18 characters to help you take down the Beast King and find your sister. This one’s got a whopping 10 endings on the menu, though I’m sure some of those are reserved for New Game+.

LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight (September 18, 2026)

The latest LEGO game finally has a Switch 2 release date. LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight is truly next level . It blends and parodies classic Batman moments from across all iterations of the caped crusader while also offering a pretty massive plastic version of Arkham to play around in. Even the combat is pretty elaborate, with inspiration from the Arkham games courtesy of development support from Rocksteady Studios.

SHINOBI: Art of Vengeance (September 24, 2026)

SEGA brought back its Shinobi series with the action platformer Art of Vengeance in 2025. We called the new release “a genuinely engaging 2D action platformer that’s beautiful to behold and even better to play” in our review , and it’ll be getting a Switch 2 port later this year.

Minecraft Dungeons II (September 29, 2026)

We called the first Minecraft Dungeons game a “fun dungeon crawler with a simple but tried-and-true set of systems.” The sequel, developed by Mojang and published by Xbox, will be launching across platforms, including Switch 2, this September . Like the first game, the block-based dungeon crawler will support both local and online multiplayer.

Yet another massive multi-platform release, IO Interactive's take on James Bond is launching on Switch 2 several months after its initial release on PC, PS5, and Xbox in late May. The game lets you play out Bond's initial recruitment and rise in the MI6 ranks, featuring Patrick Gibson as the titular spy and Lenny Kravitz as the villain Bawma .

Octopath Traveler I & II - Switch 2 Editions (October 1, 2026)

Following the release of Octopath Traveler 0 , Square Enix is releasing fresh Switch 2 editions of the original two games that defined the HD-2D style. We were big fans of both, for what it’s worth, with IGN’s Seth Macy praising how the first game “pushes JRPGs forward rather than simply paying homage to the greats” in his 9/10 review .

Remakes truly are all the rage right now. This one is a 3D reimagining of 2013’s Rayman Legends, which we called a “work of platforming genius” in our original 9.5/10 review .

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I~III] (October 8, 2026)

The Switch 2 will be getting fresh editions of existing Kingdom Hearts games, which will replace the existing ‘ Cloud streaming’ versions that were available on the Switch. Those Cloud versions were notoriously… not great, so here’s to hoping this gives everyone a better shot at the series ahead of Kingdom Hearts 4 . The three collections will be available individually or as one big bundle.

Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen (October 9, 2026)

Capcom’s RPG sequel is getting a new ‘Dark Arisen’ edition with fresh content and QOL improvements as it launches on the Switch 2. Jarrett Green reviewed the game for IGN when it was first released on PC, saying that it’s more than anything “a retelling and reimplementation of… wonderful ideas from the 2012 cult-classic.”

For the cozy gamers, The Witch’s Bakery places you in control of Lunne, a young witch who’s opening a new bakery in Paris. In the vein of something like Dave the Diver, each in-game day is split into multiple phases of managing your bakery and exploring the town while also using your magic to help your friends.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse (October 15, 2026)

The first 2D Castlevania game in almost 20 years narratively follows Castlevania 3: Dracula’s Curse, taking place a little over decade after that one’s story (which also serves as inspiration for the animated Netflix series). Mitchell Saltzman got the chance to preview the game for IGN , with particular praise for the combat, saying there’s “plenty of room to carve out your own personal playstyle thanks to the variety of weapons, Arcana, and relics.”

Tales of Eternia Remastered (October 16, 2026)

Tales of Eternia is getting a remake and returning to its original title. Previously localized as Tales of Destiny II in North America, Eternia was first released for the PS2 back in the 2000 as the third game in Namco’s Tales series.

Nintendo Switch Sports: Resort (October 22, 2026)*

In the tradition of what I consider some all-time greats, Wii Sports and Wii Sports Resort, Nintendo recently announced Nintendo Switch Sports: Resort . The Switch 2 exclusive will feature 12 sports, a mix of classics like bowling and tennis as well as new sports like thumb wrestling, that use a combination of the Switch 2’s motion and mouse controls.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort (Physical Edition)

Final Fantasy Resonance (October 22, 2026)

This new Final Fantasy game technically adapts the FF mobile game Brave Exvius that was discontinued in 2025. More notably, however, it’s the first Final Fantasy game to embrace the new HD-2D graphics system popularized by modern classics like Octopath Traveler.

IGN’s own Michael Higham got the chance to check out the first couple of hours of gameplay, so you can learn more about how this one blends new and old Final Fantasy traditions in our hands-on preview .

One Piece: Grand Gourmet (October 23, 2026)

Yep, it’s a One Piece cooking game. This one feels like a real throwback to the glory days of Flash games, which I deeply appreciate. The management sim puts you in charge of a restaurant, going on expeditions to acquire new ingredients and recipes while encountering over 400 characters from one of the greatest manga (and anime) series of all time.

This third-person action shooter puts you in control of 17-year-old Reona Minazuki, a professional ‘Diver’ that explores deadly ‘Anomaly Zones’ for the government while searching for her lost friend. The Steam listing offers the rather interesting description that the game is “steeped in the atmosphere of liminal spaces and Showa-era retro aesthetics.”

Hello Kitty Party Land (October 29, 2026)

Not too long after we got our hands on Hello Kitty Island Adventure, the iconic Sanrio character is returning for yet another cute and cozy game. This one is a party game in the tradition of classics like Mario Party, featuring more than 40 minigames and over 140 Sanrio characters.

If you’re familiar with Steins;Gate, potentially one of the most acclaimed anime of all time, you might be aware that it’s actually based on a visual novel dating back to 2009. That visual novel is getting the good old remake treatment , which will include the addition of new endings.

Metaphor Re:Fantazio (November 12, 2026)

This new IP from Atlus, best known for the SMT and Persona series, features similar mechanics around turn-based combat and social links. Instead of playing as a high schooler, though, you take on the role of Will, a young man who seeks to bring justice to a fantasy world facing its first version of an election. We gave the game a solid 9/10 when it first dropped on PC, and it even landed as our top RPG of 2024 .

This collection will come with 16 classic Barbie games that were originally released between 1991 and 2007, as well as one unreleased game, Barbie: Vacation Adventure. Funnily enough, this happens to be one of the only games daring enough to announce a release date in the November crossfires of GTA 6 .

Xenoblade Chronicles 3 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition (December 3, 2026)

In the lead-up to Xenoblade Genesis, an entirely new game in DADSS’s iconic RPG series, Xenoblade Chronicles 3 is getting the Switch 2 edition treatment. The port will also be available as a digital upgrade pack for anyone who already owns the game. IGN’s reviewer tackled the 150-hour campaign , which he considered worth the time for “great characters and addictive tactical combat.”

Upcoming Switch 2 Games With Unknown Release Dates

There are plenty more Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 games in development that don’t have a solid release date yet. Here are some more games we know are on the way, including the highly-anticipated 10th generation of Pokémon :

Professor Layton and the New World of Steam – 2026

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (Remake) - 2026

Final Fantasy VII Revelation - Spring 2027
