articles.title: Don't Skip Your Chance to Compete in The UNO Championship Series, With a $50,000 Grand Finale Prize
articles.summary: How good are you at UNO? Toy company Mattel is announcing the UNO World Championship Series, which will offer a $50,000 grand prize.
articles.body:
How good are you at UNO? This year, toy company Mattel is announcing the UNO World Championship Series, which will take the fast-paced card game to the world stage with a $50,000 grand prize.

Fancy your chances? Taking a shot at the tournament is as easy as joining in via the UNO! Mobile app, or turning up to in-person qualifiers to be held across the country in Orlando (October 3), Chicago (October 10) and Los Angeles (October 17).

Successful contestants will then compete on the world stage in the UNO World Championship grand final, broadcast live from L.A. on November 11, and available to watch globally via Twitch.

If the honor of being crowed the UNO World Champion isn't enough of a draw (pun intended), then the $50,000 prize money will likely sweeten the deal (sorry).

"At its core, UNO has always been about creating unforgettable moments around the table from epic comebacks to game-changing Draw 4s," Katie Buford, VP and Global Head of Mattel Games said. "The 2026 UNO Championship Series Tournament brings that excitement to the biggest stage yet, giving fans around the world a front-row seat as elite players battle it out to become this year's UNO champion."

Can't make it to L.A.? No worries. If you want to up your UNO game to the championship level then Mattel is launching a range of prize-worthy products for you to play with at home. These include the UNO Championship Series Tournament Set ($19.99) which includes a snazzy UNO set, scoring pad and gold trophy.

A separate UNO Championship Series Belt ($19.99) will also be available, as will a Championship Series Card Shuffler ($19.99). For the pros, the UNO Championship Series Expanded Tournament Set ($27.99) is the ultimate offering, with a more robust gold trophy for the champ.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Marvel’s Wolverine Limited-Edition PS5, DualSense Controller, and Console Covers Are Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Marvel's Wolverine for PS5 is getting the royal treatment, with limited-edition PS5 consoles, covers, and controllers up for preorder now.
articles.body:
Update 11:56 a.m. ET: The controller is now live on Amazon , but not the console bundle. These items are selling out quickly. If you want one and you see it in stock, grab it before it's gone.

Marvel’s Wolverine comes out on September 15, and on that same day Sony is also releasing a handful of new Wolverine-themed pieces of PlayStation 5 hardware. There’s a limited-edition PS5 Digital Edition bundle, some console covers, and a DualSense Wireless Controller, all decked out in black and either classic “Battle Yellow” or “Adamantium” white. They're all available for preorder on PlayStation Direct , with the controller and console bundle available at a handful of other retailers. Read on for the details.

DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Digital Edition – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition Bundle

DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Console Covers – Battle Yellow Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition

For those with no time to read blurbs, you can scroll through the catalog above to find the Wolverine-themed hardware for you.

The Battle Yellow controller is bold and very “Wolverine-y.” I love it. It features three jagged yellow claw slashes across the touchpad and left grip, with some gray weathering on either side. The sticks and bottom portion of the controller are yellow, as are the shapes on the face buttons and the directions on the D-pad.

PS5 Digital Edition – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition Bundle

If you want a new PS5, you can preorder this bundle, which includes the Wolverine-themed PS5 Digital console, plus the yellow-and-black controller, plus a digital code for Marvel’s Wolverine.

The console has an etching of the X-Men hero’s angry, yelling face at the top, with a triple slash going diagonally down the side of the machine. The whole thing is yellow and black, just like Wolverine’s costume. The controller is the same one available separately (see above).

DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

This metallic white color scheme is inspired by Wolverine's alloy-infused skeleton. It's also a PS Direct exclusive in the US and the UK , or Smyths Toys in Ireland for €84.99.

PS5 Console Covers – Battle Yellow Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

Anyone who already has a PS5 Slim can pick up a set of Wolverine-themed console covers instead of buying the whole bundle. The standard PS5 console covers come with all the pieces you need to deck out your Slim PS5, regardless of whether you have the digital or disc edition.

PS5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

If you have a PS5 Pro and you like the look of the yellow design, you can get these console covers. It includes panels for the standard digital console, as well as the disc drive attachment.

PS5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

If you have a PS5 Pro and you don’t care for yellow (or just prefer your gaming hardware to come in more muted hues), you can pick up this set of console covers that are metallic white instead of yellow.

And of course if you want to play the game at launch, you can preorder it, too. Check out our Marvel’s Wolverine preorder guide for full details on what comes in each edition.

articles.title: This robot vacuum solves my kitchen stool problem
articles.summary: Mova’s V70 Ultra Complete features an articulating mop arm that reaches under kitchen stools and around chairs.
articles.body: Robot vacuums are great at keeping your floors clean, but there are a few areas they fall down on the job — stairs being one. Another is chairs and stools. You know the scenario: You have a row of stools at a kitchen table, or chairs tucked under a dining table, and the robovac just can’t get in and around them, leaving a dust bunny bonanza. Plus, as these are generally areas where you eat, crumbs and food debris can quickly accumulate.  Of course you can move the chairs out to let the robot roam, but then the chair legs are still grungy, and you’ve had to do half the work. Mova has a solution. [Image: This is the first robot vacuum I’ve tested with a mop that extends out on an arm to reach into tighter spaces. Its latest robot vacuum and mop — the V70 Ultra Complete ($1,299.99), launching today — features a mop on an articulating arm that can reach almost 7 inches out from the robot, along with a side brush that extends 5 inches. Combined with its relatively compact size, these appendages allow the V70 to clean under and around the stool legs at my kitchen counter, extending its mop to get up to the edges of each leg and using its brush to sweep up debris under the stools. It was impressive to watch it work. [Video: Mova V70 Ultra Complete testing] After about 5 minutes on max suction, the Mova demolished the dust bunnies under my counter thanks to its 42,000Pa suction and dual roller brushes, and the area around the stools was squeaky clean. I can also see the mop arm being handy at getting the grime just under the fridge, along the TV console, and in those hard-to-reach corners. [Product: Mova V70 Ultra Complete | Mova is a sub-brand of Dreame, the company that pioneered one of my favorite mopping solutions: the mop splits. This is where the mop pads extend outwards from underneath the robot to get along baseboards and edges better. The Mova V70 takes that concept to the next level, adding a robotic mop arm that can reach out and scrub under and around things much like you would when cleaning by hand.  Mova isn’t the only one doing this. Dreame showed its version of this technology earlier this year on the X60 Pro, but with what appears to be a much larger mop and a more maneuverable arm. It hasn’t launched in the US yet. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I have only spent a day testing the Mova V70, but I really like this innovation; it’s a more useful application of a robotic appendage than picking up shoes or sprouting legs to climb stairs.  The V70 comes with a multifunction base station that cleans and dries its mop and empties its bin, and it doesn’t use disposable bags; instead, it has a canister you just empty over the trash when full. It uses lidar for navigation along with cameras for obstacle detection, and it can lift itself up over thresholds of around 3 and a half inches and remove its mops when vacuuming carpet. At $1,300, it’s one of Mova’s more expensive models, and its build quality isn’t as premium as Dreame’s $1,500 flagship X60 Max Ultra Complete. But its compact size and impressive mopping skills make it worth checking out if grungy floors under your tables and counters are a problem you want a robot to solve. Photos and video by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: The Pixel 11 isn’t the best Pixel of 2026, but it’s the smartest buy
articles.summary: Our review of the standard Google Pixel 11 is here. It’s easier to recommend than the 11 Pro, so long as superior image quality isn’t a top priority.
articles.body: It’d be easy to overlook the Pixel 11. Want the best cameras? The Pixel 11 Pro is your answer. Want the best bargain? The Pixel 10A is still a great deal. But the Pixel 11 might be the sweet spot in Google’s lineup this year. With 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, it delivers the same performance as the base Pixel 11 Pro for $899 — $200 less. And while it’s $400 more than the Pixel 10A, it has a faster processor, more RAM and storage, Qi2 charging, and a telephoto lens. It’s also the cheapest way to experience what’s actually new about the Pixel 11 series. With the hardware basically unchanged from the Pixel 10 except for new colors and a thinner camera bar, the spotlight this year has shifted to software, specifically features that aim to take full advantage of what most Pixel fans like about their phones: the cameras and special features that make the phones just a bit more helpful. Last year, we said Google’s Pixel 10 was priced fairly at $799, and that it’d be greedy for buyers to expect more from it. Well, RAMageddon happened, and everyone’s prices went up. The new Pixel 11 starts at $899 and has mostly the same specs. It adds a few exclusive software features that mostly make up for it and doubles the base storage. I guess it’d be greedy to expect much more from this one, too. [Product: Google Pixel 11 | The Pixel 11 looks, feels, and performs similarly to the $1,099 11 Pro. The Pro has a brighter, higher-resolution screen and much more powerful ultrawide and telephoto cameras, but the 11 is just as good in nearly every other way. It has the same Tensor G6 processor, and it even has the same amount of RAM as the base model Pro phone (though the more expensive Pro configurations have 16GB). In day-to-day use, I didn’t notice any performance issues owing to the smaller amount of RAM on the 11, though it’s possible that the newer processor balanced it out. Google didn’t hold back any of the software features from this model, either. As someone who doesn’t upgrade their phone unless they have to (I’m still very happy with my Pixel 9 Pro), I was skeptical that some of the phones’ most intriguing new camera features — Camera Looks and Magic Capture — would be enough to tempt me. Unfortunately for those like me who are holding off on upgrading for as long as possible, both features are rad. Like last year, the 11 has a 48MP main camera, 13MP ultrawide, and 10.8MP 5x telephoto, all of which are smaller and lower resolution than the sensors on the Pro phones. My Pixel 9 Pro’s wide and ultrawide lenses are roughly on par with the 11 Pro’s, and quite a bit more capable than the Pixel 11’s. But in the past week of testing, I don’t miss them as much as I thought I would. Camera Looks in particular helped me have more fun shooting with a Pixel than I have in years. It’s satisfying to quickly swap between different sensor-level presets, and they can make a big impact on how a photo turns out. [Image: The Pixel 11 is fast enough to snag not just a good photo of a Spider-Man imposter on the Brooklyn Bridge while driving by in a car, but a great one. I’ve been a Pixel user since 2017, going from the 2 to the 3 to the 6 to the 9 Pro, almost entirely because of the cameras. I trust them to take great shots quickly and with little effort. I even brought the Pixel 2 on my honeymoon trip instead of a DSLR, and no, I don’t regret it all these years later. If you’re a serious phone photographer who spends time composing every shot, you’ll probably want to go for the Pro, but for more casual photographers like me, the quality difference isn’t that noticeable, especially with Camera Looks applied. Camera Looks has even encouraged me to slow down sometimes to put a little more effort into my composition. Camera Looks seems like Google’s realization that the Pixel’s default vibrant HDR-drenched look isn’t the best choice for every photo. Now, it’s easy to switch to the bold, slightly more muted “Digi” or the black-and-white “Black Tie” styles when you want to take a more impactful photo. If you like one of the looks enough to make it your default shooting style, you can lock it in. And it’s easier to make adjustments on the fly, thanks to the new quick access dials you can pin to the viewfinder. You can add dials for exposure, color temperature, and shadows. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Magic Capture — another camera feature exclusive to the 11 series — is genuinely useful. The hybrid camera mode records a video and intelligently plucks hi-res photos and video clips from it, and I used it to capture a bunch of little moments with our two-year-old at the beach and at parks. It’s convenient to have a setting that can capture the unexpected without missing a beat. You can also manually capture photos while it’s recording. However, the photos are the highlight, not the video. (The resulting video looks choppier than a standard video, as if it lacks image stabilization; it doesn’t seem like it’s meant for consumption.) I’m more the type who’d like to shoot individual photos, as it feels great to happen upon a spectacular shot. But the AI does a good enough job at capturing little moments in the action. [Image: The Pixel 11’s camera bar is a little thinner than before, and Google’s new Pixelsnap case makes it sit flat on a table. Another new software component available only on the Pixel 11 lineup is Gemini’s Proactive Assistance feature. It’s meant to handle more of the grunt work of using a phone for things like managing calendars, making reservations, and buying groceries. To actually have it do things for you, you need to give the agentic AI permission (it’s not on by default) to make changes within an array of apps, ranging from Google’s productivity suite to apps like OpenTable, Instacart, Google Messages, and more. It’s partially helpful, but like an intern that gets just enough wrong that you just feel better doing it yourself. In my back-and-forth text-a-thon with David Imel, who reviewed the 11 Pro, Proactive Assistance was more miss than hit. One of the features Google advertises is an OpenTable integration that pops up a Gemini chip to book a restaurant reservation if it sees a relevant message. We could only get it to work by being as specific and formal as possible, including the restaurant’s full name and the specific day and time. That’s not how most people type to each other.  [Image: The Pixel 11’s screen resolution is equivalent to that of the Pixel 10 as well as the Pixel 10A. Here’s another example of Proactive Assistance in action: I was able to order groceries through my grocery list in Google Keep, but only after I figured out some unstated rules. After I enabled access to both Google Keep and Instacart in Gemini’s settings, I had to adjust the title of my Google Keep list to include “Instacart” (so much for being able to use natural language). Afterward, the feature quickly connected me with a list of nearby retailers that could fulfill my order, just like it does in the Instacart app. Proactive Assistance is intriguing, but I hope it gets better. You can read more about the feature’s quirks in David’s review; for now, it’s not worth upgrading for.  [Image: Google’s latest Pixel looks similar to its predecessor, but that’s not a bad thing. When I bought the Pixel 9 Pro two years ago, I picked the Pro because it was much better. It had a telephoto camera, more RAM, and more special features than the standard model. And its price came in under $1,000. This year, that’s all changed. The standard Pixel 11 now has a telephoto lens and just as much RAM as the $1,099 Pro, it’ll get all the same software features, and it’s now the one with a price under four digits. If you’re serious about phone photography, the 11 Pro is probably worth it for the bigger camera sensors. However, as someone who bought the Pixel 9 Pro two years ago, the Pixel 11’s blend of good-enough hardware and compelling software feels Pro enough to me. Photography by Cameron Faulkner/ The Verge

articles.title: Pixel 11 Pro Review – Google’s Latest Flagship Smartphone Is Not Disappointing, but It’s Not Very Exciting Either
articles.summary: The Pixel 11 Pro isn’t a performance powerhouse nor does it reinvent the wheel with game-changing new features, but it’s a good phone all the same.
articles.body:
Google has rolled out its latest line of Pixel phones with the Pixel 11 family . The Pixel 11 Pro sits at the middle, offering the same smaller footprint of the Pixel 11 while getting the extra features and cameras of the Pro models. Unsurprising for 2026, it comes with a price hike over last year’s model, bringing the starting price to $1,099 while coming with less memory, though it does have a higher base storage. Let’s dig into what the new Android flagship has going for it.

The Pixel 11 Pro is a fairly standard year-on-year refresh of the Pixel 10 Pro , which was itself a pretty tame refresh of the Pixel 9 Pro. Like those models, the Pixel 11 Pro is pleasantly compact and comfortable to hold. Its physical differences from the Pixel 10 Pro are measured on the tenth-of-a-millimeter scale, and at just three grams heavier, you’d be hard-pressed to feel any difference in the hand. Its camera bar is also still a considerable protrusion (adding 4.1mm to the 8.2mm thick phone), but at least it keeps the phone from wobbling when set on a table.

There are some fresh colors. The model sent to me for testing is the Canyon colorway, a bold salmon-like orange-pink with a gorgeous copper-colored aluminum frame. There’s also a pleasant-looking Olive green colorway. The faint, minty Fog color and matte black Obsidian look quite bland, though.

The Pixel 11 Pro sticks with largely the same materials for durability, with Gorilla Glass Victus 2 on both sides and an aluminum frame. It should be pretty sturdy, but I wouldn’t consider it even remotely hard to damage, having damaged plenty of phones quite easily over the years. There’s a new coating on the display to boost scratch resistance, and seeing scratches on the back from my short time testing but none of the front makes me think it might be helping. The Pixel 11 Pro still trods out the same IP68 protection against dust and water ingress, which should be plenty sufficient for most, though still lags behind the IP69 that the now-belly-up OnePlus had been offering on its even cheaper flagship.

Of the phone’s marquee features, the “new” HiLight feature is perhaps the lamest of all. It doubles as a camera flash and replaces the temperature sensor (even though that sensor happily sat alongside the flash in prior models). HiLight is also simply a case of Google digging up the dead and trodding them out in worse fashion. My first Android phone was a Sharp Aquos SH-01D in 2012, and it had a notification indicator light that I could set up to display different colors depending on the app giving me a notification. In 2012, the customization was already more granular than what Google is offering on its premium handset in 2026.

HiLight only lets you see a light while you’re talking to Gemini or when favorited contacts call you through the default phone app – tough luck if you use WhatsApp, Signal, or anything else as your default communication method, or if want HiLight to glow for texts from favorited contacts, too. With only five colors (if you count white as a color) to choose from to help identify specific contacts, you’ll run into a wall as soon as you have a lot of favorited contacts, and the purpose of HiLight could quickly be undermined.

The Nothing Phone has a similar feature with its customizable dot matrix animations that I find far more compelling. Never mind that with OLED displays, a similar feature could be made to run in Do Not Disturb mode such that small calling cards for favorite contacts or important apps could appear unobtrusively to have the same effect without needing a special piece of added hardware that will probably just get dumped two generations down the line anyway.

The display on the Pixel 11 Pro is hardly anything new, but that’s not a bad thing. It’s still a gorgeous 6.3-inch OLED capable of variable refresh rates from 1 to 120Hz and a new peak brightness up to 3,600 nits. That’s a minor improvement on last year’s model and not likely to make a meaningful difference, especially as you won’t be seeing those over-3000-nit brightness levels in day-to-day use unless you love to have the screen facing the sun.

The speakers aren’t a great match for the display. While the bottom speaker puts out a good deal of volume, the earpiece speaker is so much weaker that the stereo sound hardly feels like stereo. There’s enough volume to listen to a podcast or video while poking around a small room, but that’s about the extent of it.

The phone still offers a fingerprint sensor baked into the display as well as facial recognition. I’ve found both quick and reliable for unlocking the phone.

The Pixel 11 Pro also continues to operate using eSIM exclusively. It’s a minor bugbear, as I find eSIM a convenient option , but it becomes limiting to only have eSIM.

The phone’s connectivity is solid with the typical 5G alongside Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0, keeping up with the times. It also supports satellite connections when you’re remote and don’t have a terrestrial signal. The USB-C port handles charging, 10Gbps data, and can link out to displays to run a desktop mode. Oddly, the phone doesn’t automatically bring up a trackpad to navigate the desktop environment, leaving me to find a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard to get up and running.

The Pixel 11 Pro comes running Android 17 and will get 7 years of software and security updates. This has been Google’s promise for a few generations now, and it’s paired with assurances that the phones will get better over time thanks to special feature updates. I’ve known too many people who’ve had the power buttons fall off their Pixel phones within a couple years of ownership to think much of this promise anymore, never mind that the performance of the Pixel phones tends to lag behind flagship rivals and will be sorely wanting as time passes and the demands of modern software increase.

One of the new features of the Pixel 11 line is Google Keyboard's Rambler feature, a beefed-up version of speech-to-text that is designed to let you just kind of talk at it, tidying up the speech and letting you make revisions on the fly. One downside is that it doesn't show live output, so you have to wait until it's done processing to see what it's done, which can make checking it more of a chore. In testing it proved fairly reliable even as I stumbled over some of my speech. Unfortunately, this feature uses online processing for full functionality, which becomes a double shame when considering that Google could likely have made it an Android-wide feature instead of a Pixel 11 series exclusive.

Another feature Google has implemented is its Camera Looks feature. These let you snap photos with several different preset looks that handle photo processing differently, and you can make fine-tuned adjustments to each of the looks. Having an option like this certainly seems like a fine addition, though at a certain point simply shooting RAW and having the option to make whatever adjustments you want afterward might be the most sensible thing. And for casual photographers, this feature will probably feel like nothing more than simple filters.

The final big feature is Magic Capture, which basically lets you record a video carelessly and then will automatically scan through it and pull out photos (the idea being that you can then pay more attention to the real world and less to the phone). It appeared to do what it promised and served as a good way of grabbing a selfie with the rear sensor, too.

Google isn’t out here making a name for itself where raw performance is concerned. Its Tensor chips are not in that game, and the Tensor G6 is no exception. For raw speed and gaming performance, it’s much better to turn to something like the OnePlus 15 or RedMagic 11 Pro. The Pixel 11 Pro has plenty of muscle for day-to-day operation and doesn’t feel slow in general use. Gaming is another matter.

The Pixel 11 Pro got pretty toasty compiling shaders for Neverness to Everness over the course of about 10 minutes. From there, running the game at Balanced settings, it managed generally smooth visuals but had frequent hitches, especially in combat when using special moves or switching characters. With the game's Cinematic settings, hitches were even more frequent while simply wandering the game world. From a cold start, the game still hitched a bit while playing, and after 10 minutes, the phone had gotten a bit hot to hold and was hitching even more in gameplay.

Frankly, I was surprised it ran the game at Cinematic settings at all. The phone is still using a PowerVR GPU, which in last year’s model was a huge step backward for the phone’s performance. This go-around, it’s still certainly not a great gaming phone, but it’s passable.

Google finally bumped up the base storage of the phone to 256GB, though where all of the Pixel 10 Pro models had 16GB of memory, the Pixel 11 Pro starts out with just 12GB. It’s a shortcoming you probably won’t feel in practice, but it may start to hurt down the line.

The Pixel 11 Pro wields an unimpressive 4850mAh battery, which is a hair smaller than the prior phone’s 4870mAh. It’s still good for all-day use, but two full days may be a stretch depending on how heavy a user you are. The phone tops up at 30W over a wired connection, but can also use Wireless Qi2 charging at 25W, which is a solid step up over the 15W of the Pixel 10 Pro.

Unfortunately, during the initial testing period, my usual suite of benchmarks was unavailable for the phone, so I’ll have to circle back with results. That said, based on the gaming performance and history of Tensor chips, it's a safe bet that results will fall well behind phones running the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5.

The Pixel 11 Pro made a few tweaks to the Pixel 10 Pro’s camera system, opting for slightly larger sensors in a few cases but sticking to the same resolutions and apertures all around. The biggest change was in the telephoto sensor, which got a much bigger sensor that’s a boon for shooting in darker conditions and contending with its already narrow aperture. Here’s what the Pixel 11 Pro packs:

50MP Wide, 1/1.3" sensor, f/1.68, Laser AF, OIS, EIS

48MP ultrawide, 1/2.51" sensor, f/1.7, 123-degree FOV

48MP telephoto, 1/1.95" sensor, f/2.8, 5x optical, OIS, EIS

Unsurprisingly, the camera system is an all around potent mix. Up close, the main sensor is happy to capture a ton of detail with natural colors and a satisfying background blur. The tele sensor can step in for close ups as well and makes for some crisp details on subjects that might not usually make it easy to get so close.

For larger subjects, the main and ultra-wide work well together. Colors are consistent between the two, making different shots of the same subject appear like a cohesive set. The wide aperture of the ultra-wide also helps avoid running into too much noise when shooting in darker environments.

The telephoto sensor proves a fairly powerful tool, but not nearly as capable as the marketing claims. Out to 10x, the zoom still looks great and gets in pretty close on far off subjects. After that, it starts to show softness and heavy digital correction, so 30x starts to look flat and beyond that becomes simply artificial. This is made perfectly apparent by zooming into far off signage. Looking at a parking sign far enough to require the max zoom level showed me reimagined visuals and an alien script. The phone saves both the original snap and the enhanced versions at this distance, and though the originals can be quite blurry, they can still have better detail than what the enhancement invents. One car license plate in my shot clearly had a “9” showing in the original photo, but the enhanced version obliterated it.

Pixel 11 Pro – Zoom Enhanced Comparisons

Selfies look decent, but I found them a little bit softer than I would have expected from a 42MP sensor. The focus seemed soft, and the fine detail of my facial hair was simply blurred together rather than standing out.

Mark Knapp is a contributing freelancer for IGN covering everything electronics and gaming hardware. He has over 10 years of experience in the tech industry with bylines at PCMag, Reviewed, CNET, and more. Find Mark on Twitter @Techn0Mark or BlueSky at @Techn0Mark .

articles.title: The Pixel 11 Pro is a great phone, no thanks to its flashiest new features
articles.summary: Forget HiLight and Proactive Assistance. The Pixel 11 Pro is at its best with focused new tools that actually work.
articles.body: Google is trying to get you off your phone. The Pixel 11 Pro is “A Phone Designed to Help You Use It Less,” the company promises. It can proactively help you book restaurant reservations, take the best frames from a video, and help you voice-text significantly faster. The pitch is that the new features bundled with the Pixel 11 series of phones can help fix your relationship with technology — one that Google knows has badly degraded in recent years. But the hardware of the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL is very similar to last year’s models — and in at least one case, a downgrade — so those software features are pretty much the entire pitch.  Over the last week testing the 11 Pro, I’ve been trying them all to see how much they can help me put my phone down. Like many experiences with Google software, when they work, they are genuinely helpful. But getting them to work often requires a very narrow set of circumstances that some Google engineer probably dreamed up in the “society if” utopia lab. [Product: Google Pixel 11 Pro | [Product: Google Pixel 11 Pro XL | The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are minor hardware updates compared to last year’s Pixel 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL. They both get brighter 3,600-nit screens. Their charging has been upgraded, with faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W when wireless. The 5x optical telephoto camera has a bigger sensor that Google says enables 30 percent more light intake. Storage now starts at 256GB, instead of 128GB. And there’s also a fancy new “notification light,” which I’ll get to in a bit.  Unfortunately, these upgrades come with a downgrade too, for the base model at least. The 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL now start with less RAM: 12GB compared to the 16GB that came standard last year, the same amount as the regular Pixel 11. I’m testing the 16GB / 512GB model, so unfortunately I can’t tell you if the RAM decrease is noticeable. That base model is also $100 more expensive than last year, too, at $1,099.   With such minor spec changes, Google has gone all in on software this year. And this time, that software’s primary purpose is to get you off your phone, or at least get tedious tasks done faster so you can get back to your life. [Image: Proactive Assistance popping up inside Google Messages. Perhaps the largest push in this direction is the Pixel 11’s new “Proactive Assistance” feature. This is a set of dynamic chips that appear when certain interactions happen on your phone, like a friend asking what your schedule looks like next week or if you booked that table at a restaurant yet. For the most basic interactions, like checking availability or adding an event to my calendar, I found Proactive Assistance really helpful. I practically live inside my calendar, and text conversations about scheduling are common. When my friend Marc texted me asking when I was available next week, Gemini popped up and suggested checking my calendar for times. Outside of simple scenarios like that, though, Proactive Assistance gets less reliable. One of Google’s key examples is letting Gemini book a dinner reservation for you if you’re chatting about heading out to eat, but I had to receive a text with an extremely specific string of information to get it to work — and even then it only worked sometimes. For example, receiving the text “Can you make a reservation at Frankie Spuntino next Saturday at 7pm?” surfaced a chip to agentically try to make the reservation. But if the message doesn’t include the date or time, it won’t invoke anything at all. Most of the time when the chip does show up, it disappears the moment I reply. Occasionally it will stick around if the AI thinks we’re still talking about the restaurant, but those instances were few and far between. I wish Google would keep the chip around for at least a few messages, or have it float around the messages in some way. One promise of large language models is the ability to understand what you mean and remove the requirements for smart keywords, so it’s odd that explicit keywords are still necessary to get so much of Proactive Assistance to work. I can see what Google is trying to do with this and I can maybe see a future where it gets refined, but as it stands, it’s simply too inconsistent. Plus, I had to manually toggle on Proactive Assistance and add OpenTable to connected apps in settings, which I just don’t think most people will know to do. As my colleague Cameron Faulkner puts it, “You need to be proactive to get Proactive Assistance to work.” Proactive Assistance is advertised as working with other scenarios too, like surfacing your flight information when someone asks what time your flight is or bringing up the right photo when someone asks for it. But both of these scenarios either failed or were inconsistent for me. Asking when my flight is supposed to land surfaced nothing even though I have flight information in my Gmail, and when my friend asked for a photo of me from 2024, it surfaced photos from 2024, but none of me. It’s disappointing that this feature only works in such narrow circumstances. I can see the vision, but the execution just isn’t there yet. [Image: The HiLight LED. Another feature that got a lot of marketing hype but flatlined on its delivery is HiLight. You may have noticed the temperature sensor is missing on the Pixel 11 Pro. Instead, Google has replaced it with a multicolored LED ring hidden inside the flash that can glow when different things are happening on your phone. Again, in concept, I love this idea. Google wants you to be living your life, with your phone placed face down on the table so it can’t distract you unless HiLight notifies you of something you need to pay attention to. In practice, HiLight is so badly executed that it’s frankly embarrassing. Right now, HiLight can glow for exactly two things. First, it will glow and animate when you’re speaking with Gemini, but only while your phone is face down on the table. These are two things I do not do very often. When I use Gemini, I’m generally typing to it, and when I do use Gemini voice mode, my phone is in my hand or sitting screen up. If this was just one of the many things HiLight could light up for, I wouldn’t find it so offensive. But at the moment, the only other thing HiLight will glow for is for calls from your favorite contacts. I wish I was kidding. [Image: The only options for HiLight. If I’m getting a call from a favorite contact, I just want my phone to ring. Again, if it was just an additional feature, then sure, I guess. I don’t mind having an additional indicator that a favorite is calling me while my phone is face down. But if the call is coming through anyway, it’s really not that much effort to turn the phone over and see who it is. To make it worse, you can only choose from five colors, and one of them is white! Customizable RGB LEDs were a feature we lost long ago, but when we did have it, it was almost always possible to map to just about any notification you wanted: red for a new email, green for a WhatsApp message. Google has confirmed that it’s looking to add text notifications from favorite contacts to HiLight, but why not just make it customizable to any app? This feels like such a missed opportunity, and it’s wild to me that it wasn’t better thought out before launch. Right now, it’s just acting like my flash, like it’s always been. There are some new features that I’m finding genuinely useful that do help me stay in the moment, though. I was most pleasantly surprised by Rambler, a souped-up voice-to-text tool powered by Gemini. Rambler removes the filler words that voice-to-text would normally pick up, does proper grammar and punctuation without explicitly asking for it, and will even rewrite misspeaks mid-recording. The speed of the Pixel’s voice-to-text has been one of its strong suits ever since Google started using its own Tensor chips on the Pixel 6, but Rambler makes this even better, to the point where I’m dictating the text on my phone whenever I have the opportunity. It is a genuinely great feature, saves me time, and almost makes it feel like I’m having a conversation in real time while texting. [Image: Using Rambler on the Pixel 11 Pro. As is tradition, Google also introduced a bunch of new camera features this year, and perhaps the most prominent is Magic Capture. The feature is front and center in the camera app right next to the photo and video modes, which tells you something about how confident Google is in it. Start a Magic Capture, point it at what’s happening, and when you’re done recording, Gemini will do some processing and pull out what it considers the best photos and video clips from the session. During the Made by Google keynote last week, Google demoed the feature by recording some people shooting hoops on a basketball court. In the demonstration, Google said you could simply hold your phone and let it record while you take in the moment with your eyes. I have tried this exact scenario quite a few times, and let me tell you, it is extremely difficult to keep your subject in frame if you’re not staring at your screen. Magic Capture did a great job of pulling relevant images and clips from my recordings when I was making sure to keep my subject in frame by, you know, staring at my screen, but unless you have your phone mounted on a tripod or something, it’s naive to think you can ignore your phone completely. That caveat aside, I really like this feature. I take a lot of videos on my phone, but I’m much more likely to revisit pictures. With Magic Capture, I can have both. The main caveat seems to be that stabilization isn’t as good on the clips it cuts compared to clips you’d take in video mode. Even so, I think Magic Capture will be useful for parents trying to capture moments of their kids, without needing to work so hard to get the perfect smile for a photo. Instead of marketing this feature as something that lets you be in the moment by not looking at your phone at all, it would probably be better to pitch it as something that will automatically grab great photos and short video clips for you, and all you need to do is point your phone and hit record. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: While Magic Capture took most of the spotlight in Google’s keynote, maybe the most discussed photo upgrade this year is Camera Looks. I did a whole interview with Google’s camera chief about this feature going deep into how the new system was made, and there’s a lot of potential in the execution. Camera Looks is a new photography feature you can think of similar to Fujifilm’s film simulations, which let its cameras emulate different film styles on the JPGs they put out. On the Pixel 11 series, there are four modifications of the standard camera, with Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla giving subtle tweaks to your image. But if you want to get more out there, there are six additional creative looks, called Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal. Each of the looks can be modified to your liking, with adjustable settings like contrast, highlights, shadows, vibrance, tint, warmth, sharpness, and grain. What makes this a really interesting feature to me is that Google is adjusting the amount of computational processing it’s doing at capture, based on the settings you choose; it’s not just applying filters later. For example, the Digi mode will do less frame stacking and the Minimal mode will apply less sharpness and contrast. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I really dig the looks, even right out of the box. They span from basic edits to quite inspired, and if you’re looking for something that gives you the “film simulation look” straight out of camera, these definitely deliver. It was high time Google added some more creative looks to the Pixel, especially considering it doesn’t have nearly as robust a third-party camera ecosystem as the iPhone. I’ve personally made the Minimal mode permanent on my phone for its unsharpened, minimally contrasty look, occasionally switching to Classic, but after testing them all, I think Velvet and Editorial will get a lot of use, since they have the most “film aesthetic” of the bunch. With less processed photos, you can actually see texture in photos, which is normally washed away by noise reduction algorithms. Overall camera quality on the Pixel 11 Pro series is great this year, and practically the only reason to pick up a Pro Pixel over the standard 11, aside from wanting a larger phone, in the case of the XL. The primary sensor is technically new, but Google tells me it’s the same size as last year and was swapped in because it uses slightly less power. The biggest camera hardware change is the new larger telephoto sensor, which Google says captures more light, and I can tell. Telephoto cameras are usually the weakest link in a smartphone’s camera arsenal, but even at 10x zoom, which is a 2x crop of the telephoto sensor, it was hard to notice any significant quality degradation. Plus, the transition between sensors is much smoother now, with only a very slight jump when switching between lenses. [Image: The Camera Looks interface. The Pixel 11 Pro also includes a 120x Pro Zoom mode, enabled by the new image signal processor in Tensor G6. Like the 100x Pro Zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro, Google is using generative AI to upscale your highly zoomed-in images to make them look more realistic. On objects without a lot of sharp edges this actually does a pretty good job, and Google will give you both the non-AI-enhanced and enhanced versions so you can see the difference. I was in Spain during last week’s solar eclipse, and the Pixel 11 Pro did a good job of turning a zoomed-in photo of the moon from a blurry mess into something that looked good enough to elicit responses of awe when I posted it in Slack. But that was a relatively simple image, and shots with a lot more detail often look like an early AI-generated image, with skewed angles and edges, garbled text, and muddy tones. I’d only really use this if you needed to see information you can’t see with your normal eyes, not for artistic purposes. [Image: [Image: The Pixel 11 Pro also gets a new, faster Night Sight, which Google says is about three times faster on average than the Pixel 10 Pro. In testing, most Night Sight images I took only needed to be held for one second, and I got all the same benefits you got from holding the phone for three or more seconds previously. This is the kind of quality-of-life update I love to see, and I’m glad Google is continuing to improve here. I love Rambler, Magic Capture, and Camera Looks. If you’re looking to upgrade your phone this year, they’re legitimately great features. But after a week of use, it’s clear to me that the Pixel 11 Pro is not yet smart enough to help me use my phone less, despite what Google claims. Proactive Assistance is only bound to save you a few seconds and a few taps compared to just opening the apps and doing the steps yourself. If you were hoping for the Pixel 11 Pro would help address your phone addiction, that’s probably not going to happen. But if you’re looking for a phone with the best voice-to-text on the market, great cameras with good built-in style, and solid hardware, the Pixel 11 Pro delivers.  Photography by David Imel / The Verge
